The Fed's discretion is irrelevant — markets ignore policy decisions in the modern era completely
The Fed's discretion is perfect — every decision since 2008 has been exactly correct and necessary
context: Volcker's late-career writing emphasized that the Fed had drifted from its early-1980s discipline. He saw the post-2008 expansion of Fed powers as a serious institutional risk. The contrast between Volcker's 1981 willingness to take political pain and the post-2008 Fed's instinct for accommodation tells the story of two different institutional cultures.

question: Milton Friedman's 1980 PBS series *Free to Choose* (10 episodes) reached millions of households. The companion book sold over a million copies. The series argued voluntary exchange and price signals produce flourishing where central planning produces ruin. What did the title mean?
answer: Free to choose — individuals decide how to spend their own time and money in voluntary exchange
choices: Free to choose — individuals decide how to spend their own time and money in voluntary exchange
Free to choose — voters select their preferred political leaders through regular democratic elections
Free to choose — workers select whichever federal welfare program suits their individual needs
Free to choose — central planners select which industries should be nationalized in any given year
context: Friedman's *Free to Choose* (1980) is one of the most-watched economics PBS series ever made. The series and book made the case for voluntary exchange and against central planning in language accessible to non-economists.

question: Thomas Sowell — Hoover senior fellow, born 1930 — has written 30+ books on economics, history, and social issues. *Knowledge and Decisions* (1980) generalized Hayek's knowledge problem to all institutions. What's his central commitment?
answer: Facts and consequences first — pursue data and second-order effects before ideological commitment
choices: Facts and consequences first — pursue data and second-order effects before ideological commitment
Theory and elegance first — economic models should be elegant before being tested against any empirical data
Politics and ideology first — economic conclusions should follow from the analyst's prior political commitments
Tradition and authority first — economic conclusions should defer to the historical mainstream consensus
context: Sowell's methodological commitment to facts-over-ideology is unusual in modern economics. His career arc — from Marxism to Chicago to free-market institutional economist — is a study in changing one's mind in response to evidence. The 'And then what?' question structures most of his popular writing.

question: Ludwig von Mises fled Vienna in 1934, reached the US in 1940, and from 1945 to 1969 held an unpaid visiting position at NYU — funded by Lawrence Fertig and the William Volker Fund, not the university. Rothbard attended his Thursday seminars. Why did the 20th century's most important Austrian economist never hold a paid US faculty post?
answer: His free-market views were unacceptable — to a postwar US academy dominated by Keynesians and mathematical model-builders
choices: His free-market views were unacceptable — to a postwar US academy dominated by Keynesians and mathematical model-builders
Mises preferred unpaid posts for tax reasons — postwar US income above $5,000 was taxed at over 90 percent at the time
NYU was the only US university Mises would teach at — because of a personal friendship with the president of NYU
Mises was independently wealthy from Austrian banking — and never needed paid academic employment during his lifetime
context: The Volker Fund kept Mises in his chair for nearly 25 years. Hayek faced similar headwinds and ended up at Chicago's Committee on Social Thought, not the economics department.

question: Ludwig von Mises died October 10, 1973, in New York City at age 92. He had outlived the Austro-Hungarian Empire, two world wars, the Keynesian consensus he spent decades fighting, and even Bretton Woods (Nixon closed it August 15, 1971). What was Mises's 1949 magnum opus, his systematic treatise on praxeology?
answer: Human Action — the thousand-page treatise grounding economics in purposeful human choice
choices: Human Action — the thousand-page treatise grounding economics in purposeful human choice
Capital and Interest — Bohm-Bawerk's three-volume work on time preference theory of interest
The Road to Serfdom — Hayek's wartime polemic against central planning for a popular audience
Principles of Economics — Carl Menger's 1871 founding work establishing the Austrian school
context: Capital and Interest was Bohm-Bawerk's; Road to Serfdom was Hayek's (1944); Principles of Economics was Menger's (1871). Human Action (Yale, 1949) is Mises's magnum opus. The 1966 third revised edition is the standard reference.

question: Mises's economic method — 'praxeology' — starts from one axiom: humans act purposefully, choosing means to reach ends. From that self-evident starting point, Mises argued, all economic theory follows by logical deduction, without statistical testing. Why did he reject the rival idea that economics should look like physics with empirical data?
answer: Human action involves choice and learning — so no two situations repeat exactly, and there are no constant relationships to measure
choices: Human action involves choice and learning — so no two situations repeat exactly, and there are no constant relationships to measure
Mises had no objection in principle — but said statistical methods were too immature in 1949 to be useful for any policy work
Mises argued the action axiom was empirical — derived from psychological surveys conducted in Vienna before WWI
Mises preferred laboratory testing of economic theories — but said the cost of running controlled trials made the work impossible
context: Mises grounded praxeology in Human Action (1949). The methodological dispute pitted him against mathematical modeling and econometrics. Modern Austrians range from strict praxeologists (Hoppe) to more empirical figures (Boettke).

question: In 1912 Mises published The Theory of Money and Credit. He was 31, a private docent at the University of Vienna. The book applied marginal-utility analysis to money itself, integrating monetary theory with the broader Austrian framework. What boom-and-bust idea did it plant — later developed by Hayek into a full cycle theory?
answer: Credit expansion below the natural rate of interest causes malinvestment — which must later be liquidated in the bust
choices: Credit expansion below the natural rate of interest causes malinvestment — which must later be liquidated in the bust
Money supply has no link to prices in the short term — credit expansion lifts output without ever raising costs
Boom and bust cycles are caused by animal spirits and panic — monetary policy plays no role in generating either
Money is a veil over barter — changes in money supply leave all real economic relationships unchanged at every horizon
context: Hayek developed the cycle theory further in Prices and Production (1931). Mises's regression theorem in the same book also traced money's value back to its pre-monetary use as a commodity.

question: In 1920 Mises published 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth.' His argument: without private ownership of capital goods, no market for them exists; without that market, no money prices form; without prices, planners cannot compare alternative production methods. Mises claimed socialism is not merely inefficient — what is the stronger claim he made about it?
answer: Impossible — rational economic calculation cannot occur without price information
choices: Impossible — rational economic calculation cannot occur without price information
Workable with surveys — planners can substitute engineering estimates for prices
More efficient than markets — coordinated production beats the waste of competition
Identical to markets — Mises's 1920 paper showed both systems converge
context: The calculation debate ran for decades. Oskar Lange in the 1930s claimed planners could 'simulate' a market by trial and error. Hayek answered with the knowledge problem (1945). The 20th century settled the debate empirically.

question: In January-February 1931 the London School of Economics invited Friedrich Hayek — then 31, on the Vienna faculty — to give four lectures on capital and money. They were a direct intellectual challenge to John Maynard Keynes at Cambridge, whose Treatise on Money had appeared the previous October. What became of them?
answer: They were published that year as Prices and Production — laying out Austrian Business Cycle Theory and earning Hayek a permanent LSE chair
choices: They were published that year as Prices and Production — laying out Austrian Business Cycle Theory and earning Hayek a permanent LSE chair
They were never published — Hayek burned the manuscripts when Keynes's General Theory appeared in 1936, conceding defeat
They were published as a personal-attack pamphlet — leading to Hayek being expelled from the LSE before the academic year ended
They were published only after WWII — as part of a posthumous collected works edited by Milton Friedman in the 1970s
context: Hayek demolished Keynes's Treatise in a long Economica review (1931). Keynes responded by abandoning the Treatise and writing The General Theory (1936) on different ground. The Cambridge-LSE rivalry shaped a generation of British economics.

question: Friedrich Hayek received the Nobel in Economics on December 11, 1974. His acceptance lecture — 'The Pretense of Knowledge' — was a startling speech for a Nobel ceremony: an attack on the scientific aspirations of his own profession. What did he accuse economists of pretending?
answer: That economies can be understood and managed via data and math models — pretending to a precision and control economists do not actually possess
choices: That economies can be understood and managed via data and math models — pretending to a precision and control economists do not actually possess
That forecasts had been too pessimistic — Hayek used his speech to call for renewed confidence in central-planner growth projections
That free markets could solve every problem — Hayek used his Nobel lecture to retract his earlier work and endorse the postwar consensus
That economists deserved Nobel Prizes at all — Hayek refused the medal and donated the prize money to the Soviet Academy of Sciences
context: Hayek shared the 1974 Nobel with Gunnar Myrdal — an awkward pairing given opposite views. 'The Pretense of Knowledge' warned policymakers acting on bad theory could do more damage than letting markets adjust. Inflation was already rising; he was vindicated within years.

question: Friedrich Hayek's final book, The Fatal Conceit: The Errors of Socialism, appeared in 1988 — Hayek was 89, three years before his death. The book argued that socialism's appeal to rational, designed social order missed a deep fact about how civilization actually works. What was the 'fatal conceit'?
answer: Believing humans can rationally design an economic order — when the institutions that produced prosperity (markets, property, money) evolved without any central designer
choices: Believing humans can rationally design an economic order — when the institutions that produced prosperity (markets, property, money) evolved without any central designer
Believing socialism was historically inevitable — Hayek argued capitalism was inevitable instead, and predicted the imminent collapse of every Western government
Believing Western economists understood the USSR — Hayek argued Soviet data had been accurate and the West had underestimated Soviet output
Believing markets caused all human conflict — Hayek argued in this final book that central planning was the only path to lasting peace
context: The Fatal Conceit consolidated themes from a career — spontaneous order, the limits of reason, the evolution of moral rules. The Berlin Wall fell the next year, in November 1989. Hayek lived to see it.

question: In 1962 Murray Rothbard published Man, Economy, and State — a thousand-page treatise originally commissioned by the Volker Fund as a textbook companion to Mises's Human Action. Rothbard went further than the publisher wanted, integrating Austrian theory with a libertarian political position. He was 36. What did the book do?
answer: Reconstruct economic theory from praxeological foundations — extending and systematizing Mises's Human Action with explicit logical derivation
choices: Reconstruct economic theory from praxeological foundations — extending and systematizing Mises's Human Action with explicit logical derivation
Survey existing theories and grade each against Keynesian benchmarks — Rothbard's book was a graduate-level macroeconomics textbook
Compile statistical evidence supporting central planning — Rothbard had not yet broken from his earlier left-wing views in 1962
Defend the Federal Reserve as a stabilizing institution — Rothbard later regretted the book and removed it from his bibliography
context: Mises blurbed Man, Economy, and State as a 'masterful presentation.' The final state-chapter was cut by the publisher and later published separately as Power and Market (1970). Rothbard founded the Mises Institute in 1982.

question: From the late 1950s through the 1980s, Murray Rothbard ran private seminars from his Manhattan apartment. The 'Monday-evening seminar' typically drew a dozen participants for free-form conversation lasting until 1 or 2 a.m. Why was that informal setting historically important to Austrian economics?
answer: It transmitted Austrian theory to a generation of students — at a time when no US university would teach the material seriously
choices: It transmitted Austrian theory to a generation of students — at a time when no US university would teach the material seriously
It was open to the public for a fee — making Rothbard wealthy enough to retire from academic work entirely by the mid-1960s
It was a Communist Party USA front group — Rothbard had not yet broken from his earlier Marxist views when the seminars began
It was state-funded — the Ford Foundation paid for the seminars from 1958 to 1979 as part of a liberal arts outreach effort
context: The seminars produced future Austrian scholars including Joseph Salerno and Walter Block. Rothbard moved to UNLV in 1986. The Mises Institute's annual Mises University at Auburn carries the tradition forward.

question: Murray Rothbard published America's Great Depression in 1963 — the same year Friedman and Schwartz brought out their Monetary History of the United States. The two books reach opposite conclusions about the 1920s and 1930s. Friedman blamed the Fed for letting M2 collapse 1929-1933. What did Rothbard blame the Fed for?
answer: The 1920s credit expansion that caused the unsustainable boom — making the post-1929 collapse inevitable as malinvestments were liquidated
choices: The 1920s credit expansion that caused the unsustainable boom — making the post-1929 collapse inevitable as malinvestments were liquidated
Nothing — Rothbard's book actually defended the Fed in its 1920s policy and pinned sole blame on the Hoover administration
World War II planning — Rothbard's book said the Fed handled the 1920s and 1930s correctly but mismanaged postwar demobilization
Foreign monetary policy — Rothbard's book pinned the Depression on the Bank of England's 1925 return to gold, not on any US Fed action
context: Friedman's monetarist (Fed failed by inaction) and Rothbard's Austrian (Fed caused the boom) interpretations are not entirely opposed — both blame the Fed — but differ on what counterfactual policy would have been right. Rothbard also demolished the myth that Hoover was a hands-off free-marketeer.

question: Murray Rothbard's The Ethics of Liberty appeared in 1982 — a systematic statement of libertarian political theory grounded in self-ownership and the non-aggression principle. The book was drafted in the early 1970s but set aside for his colonial-America history. What is the core ethical claim?
answer: Every person owns themselves — using force against a peaceful person is the only action a society may rightly forbid, and any government act beyond that is illegitimate
choices: Every person owns themselves — using force against a peaceful person is the only action a society may rightly forbid, and any government act beyond that is illegitimate
Every person owes service to the political community — Rothbard's ethics combined civic republicanism with limited welfare programs for the deserving
Every person should obey democratic majorities — Rothbard's ethics centered on majority rule and held minority interests must defer to votes
Every person should follow conscience without rules — Rothbard's ethics rejected all property claims and embraced complete moral relativism
context: Rothbard's framework built on Locke's labor theory of property and natural rights traditions, sharpening the non-aggression principle into a comprehensive system. The framework remains foundational for modern libertarianism.

question: Thomas Sowell — born 1930 in Gastonia, North Carolina, raised in Harlem — was a self-described Marxist through undergrad at Harvard and his Columbia master's. Then in summer 1960 he took a Labor Department job studying minimum-wage effects on Puerto Rico. What changed his mind about benevolent government?
answer: His colleagues had no interest in whether the minimum wage actually helped workers — only in keeping the program funded — and he lost faith in benevolent intervention
choices: His colleagues had no interest in whether the minimum wage actually helped workers — only in keeping the program funded — and he lost faith in benevolent intervention
He encountered a persuasive economics paper at Harvard that fall — and converted to mainstream Keynesian economics over a single semester
He attended a private dinner with Milton Friedman in 1959 — and Friedman convinced him over one evening that Austrian theory was correct
He inherited a small fortune in 1960 — and reasoned that owning capital made socialism personally inconvenient for him as a new beneficiary
context: Sowell went on to a PhD at Chicago under George Stigler, taught at UCLA, and joined the Hoover Institution at Stanford in 1980 — where he has remained. His books are among the most widely read economics works in the world. He's still publishing at 95.

question: Thomas Sowell published Marxism: Philosophy and Economics in 1985 — a sympathetic and devastating analysis of Marx's actual writings (not the cartoon Marx of either side). Sowell, a former Marxist himself, was unusually qualified to write it. What was its central judgment?
answer: Marx's theory was internally coherent in 1867 but empirically wrong on its key predictions — the labor theory of value was abandoned by serious economics around 1870 for good reasons
choices: Marx's theory was internally coherent in 1867 but empirically wrong on its key predictions — the labor theory of value was abandoned by serious economics around 1870 for good reasons
Marx's theory was vague and contradictory — and no serious analysis could be written without first untangling the philosophical errors he had inherited from Kant
Marx's theory was empirically confirmed by Soviet experience — Sowell's book was the most pro-Marxist work ever published by a Hoover Institution scholar
Marx's theory was identical to Adam Smith's — Sowell's book argued the entire 19th-century distinction between Marx and classical economics was a fabrication
context: Sowell quotes Marx extensively and takes his arguments seriously, distinguishing his views from those of later Marxists. The 1871 marginal revolution (Menger, Jevons, Walras) replaced the labor theory of value with subjective marginal utility. Sowell's youthful Marxism gave him sympathetic access to material he later refuted.

question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock published The Calculus of Consent in 1962 — the founding work of public choice economics. The book applied self-interested rational behavior to politicians, bureaucrats, and voters — the same assumption economists had long applied to market participants. What followed?
answer: Government actors pursue their own interests like everyone else — so 'market failure justifies government' has to be checked against real political behavior, not an idealized state
choices: Government actors pursue their own interests like everyone else — so 'market failure justifies government' has to be checked against real political behavior, not an idealized state
Government actors are uniquely public-spirited — Buchanan and Tullock argued democratic accountability eliminates self-interest from political life
Government actors should be removed from economic analysis — politics and economics belong to entirely separate disciplines that must not overlap
Government actors always know best — Buchanan and Tullock recommended expanding the regulatory state as the cure for market failures of any kind
context: The Calculus of Consent gave economists tools to analyze constitutional rules, voting systems, rent-seeking, and bureaucratic incentives. Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel for this body of work. Public choice has shaped a generation of political economy.

question: James M. Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Economics 'for his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making.' He was teaching at George Mason University in Virginia, having moved there from Virginia Tech in 1983 with his Center for Study of Public Choice. What had Buchanan's work done?
answer: Brought political institutions inside economic analysis — applying the tools of choice and self-interest to constitutions and voting rules
choices: Brought political institutions inside economic analysis — applying the tools of choice and self-interest to constitutions and voting rules
Built the Keynesian fiscal-multiplier framework — providing empirical estimates of government-spending effects across all major economies
Constructed mathematical equilibrium models — proving that markets reach efficient outcomes under all known conditions
Designed the dual-mandate framework for central banks — defining how monetary policy should manage inflation and employment together
context: Buchanan's George Mason institutional base proved durable — the Center for Study of Public Choice remains a leading research hub. His later works (The Power to Tax, Constitutional Political Economy) extended the framework. The Nobel citation honored a body of work spanning four decades.

question: Gordon Tullock published 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft' in the Western Economic Journal in 1967 — a short paper that introduced what later became known as 'rent-seeking.' The idea was that competition for political privilege wastes real resources, beyond the standard 'deadweight loss' textbooks taught. What did Tullock see?
answer: Lobbyists and lawyers spend real time and money fighting for tariff and license favors — that spending is a social loss, not just a transfer from consumers
choices: Lobbyists and lawyers spend real time and money fighting for tariff and license favors — that spending is a social loss, not just a transfer from consumers
Lobbying always increases social welfare — Tullock showed that political competition produces optimal outcomes when many interest groups compete
Lobbying has no real cost — the only welfare loss from tariffs is the small triangle of deadweight loss captured by introductory textbooks
Lobbying is a victimless activity — Tullock's paper argued that no resources are wasted in political competition because all participants benefit
context: Anne Krueger gave the practice its modern name ('rent-seeking') in a 1974 American Economic Review paper, but Tullock's 1967 piece is the foundational text. The recognition reshaped how economists think about regulation, licensing, and political favor-seeking. Tullock was at the University of Virginia at the time, working alongside Buchanan.

question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960 in 1963. The chapter on the Great Depression made a startling argument: the Fed didn't just fail to stop the catastrophe — the Fed CAUSED it by letting M2 collapse roughly 33% between 1929 and 1933. What does this say about the Fed's defenders?
answer: An institution founded in 1913 to prevent banking panics presided over the worst banking collapse in US history — and was defended afterward by the profession it employs
choices: An institution founded in 1913 to prevent banking panics presided over the worst banking collapse in US history — and was defended afterward by the profession it employs
The Fed's 1929-1933 actions were textbook-perfect — Friedman and Schwartz documented the Fed's role in shortening the downturn substantially
Banks alone caused the Depression — Friedman and Schwartz absolved the Fed of any role in the contraction of money or credit during the period
Tariffs caused the Depression — Friedman and Schwartz argued in this book that the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act was the only meaningful driver of the slump
context: Friedman and Schwartz reshaped how the Great Depression is taught. Ben Bernanke, citing Friedman explicitly, took Fed chair into 2008 determined not to repeat the 1929-33 contraction — and arguably overcorrected with the rounds of QE that followed.

question: In January 1980, PBS aired the first episode of Free to Choose — a ten-part television series hosted by Milton Friedman. The companion book (co-authored with his wife Rose Friedman) became a bestseller. Friedman, then 67, traveled to Hong Kong, India, and elsewhere on camera. What was the show's project?
answer: Making the case for free markets to a general American audience — using vivid examples instead of equations to demonstrate how voluntary exchange produces results central planning cannot
choices: Making the case for free markets to a general American audience — using vivid examples instead of equations to demonstrate how voluntary exchange produces results central planning cannot
Defending the Carter administration's economic policies on national television — Friedman supported Carter's wage and price controls throughout the production
Promoting his upcoming candidacy for political office in California — Friedman ran for governor on the Libertarian ticket later that year
Critiquing Reagan's incoming economic team — Friedman recorded the show in late 1980 specifically to oppose the supply-side advisors arriving in Washington
context: Friedman won the 1976 Nobel in Economics. Free to Choose aired at a pivotal political moment — Reagan was elected in November 1980 — and helped shape public discussion of markets, regulation, and the welfare state. The series remains widely circulated. Friedman died November 16, 2006.

question: In his 1967 presidential address to the AEA ('The Role of Monetary Policy'), Milton Friedman attacked the dominant 'Phillips curve' view — the empirical claim that inflation and unemployment had a stable inverse relationship policymakers could exploit. Friedman's prediction was risky and specific. What did he say?
answer: The trade-off would break down — workers would adjust wage demands once they expected inflation, and stagflation (high inflation AND high unemployment) would result
choices: The trade-off would break down — workers would adjust wage demands once they expected inflation, and stagflation (high inflation AND high unemployment) would result
The trade-off would tighten — the Phillips relationship would become even stronger as monetary policy improved over the coming decades
The trade-off would invert — unemployment and inflation would soon move in the same direction permanently due to globalization
The trade-off had no historical basis — the Phillips curve was a 1958 statistical artifact and would never appear in any later data
context: Edmund Phelps made the same point independently in 1967. The 1970s — high unemployment combined with high inflation — vindicated Friedman and Phelps. Phelps won the 2006 Nobel for related work; Friedman had won in 1976. The Phillips curve's collapse was one of mid-century economics' most striking empirical reversals.

question: Ronald Coase published 'The Problem of Social Cost' in the Journal of Law and Economics in 1960 — the most-cited economics paper ever written. The paper challenged the standard 'externality' framework that economists from Pigou onward had relied on: factories pollute, so tax them. What did Coase say instead?
answer: If property rights are clear and transaction costs are low, parties will bargain to an efficient outcome — without needing taxes or regulation imposed from above
choices: If property rights are clear and transaction costs are low, parties will bargain to an efficient outcome — without needing taxes or regulation imposed from above
Externalities can never be resolved by private bargaining — Coase argued government taxes are the only available tool to address pollution and other spillovers
Externalities don't exist as a category — Coase showed that all economic interactions are either pure exchange or pure theft with no middle case to analyze
Externalities are always solved by lawsuits — Coase argued that courts assign damages mechanically and no party ever needs to bargain about pollution effects
context: Coase had originally written 'The Federal Communications Commission' (1959) on radio-spectrum allocation, applying the same insight. His Chicago colleagues found the argument so startling they invited him to defend it at a dinner. He persuaded them. The paper is the founding document of the field of law and economics.

question: What's now called the 'Coase theorem' wasn't named by Coase himself — Stigler coined the label in his 1966 textbook. The theorem describes the case where transaction costs are essentially zero. What does it say about who initially holds the property right?
answer: Initial allocation of the right doesn't affect the final outcome — both sides bargain until the resource ends up with whoever values it most, regardless of who started with it
choices: Initial allocation of the right doesn't affect the final outcome — both sides bargain until the resource ends up with whoever values it most, regardless of who started with it
Initial allocation must always favor the polluter — only by giving rights to factories first can the economy reach the efficient pollution level
Initial allocation must always favor the victim — only by giving rights to neighbors first can a court resolve a pollution dispute correctly under law
Initial allocation is meaningless because no bargaining is ever possible — Coase argued that all property disputes inevitably require government decree
context: Coase's actual point was the opposite of how the theorem is sometimes summarized in textbooks. He emphasized that transaction costs are NEVER zero in reality — so the institutional setup of property rights and legal rules matters enormously. The 'theorem' is a baseline; the real world is the deviation from it.

question: Ronald Coase won the 1991 Nobel in Economics 'for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure and functioning of the economy.' He was 80 years old, born in 1910 in Willesden, England. What was his early-career paper from 1937 also remembered for?
answer: 'The Nature of the Firm' — asking why firms exist at all instead of every transaction happening through market contracts, answering with transaction costs
choices: 'The Nature of the Firm' — asking why firms exist at all instead of every transaction happening through market contracts, answering with transaction costs
'The Theory of Marginal Utility' — Coase's restatement of the 1871 Austrian theory of value in modernized form for Cambridge undergraduates
'Inflation Targeting Doctrine' — Coase's early proposal for the framework now used by most central banks since the 1990s and onward
'Game Theory and the State' — Coase's foundational paper applying von Neumann's mathematics to international diplomacy
context: Coase's two great papers ('The Nature of the Firm' 1937, 'The Problem of Social Cost' 1960) span 23 years and form a coherent vision: transaction costs are everywhere in the economy and explain features (firms, regulation, property rules) that earlier economists had taken for granted. Coase died September 2, 2013, at age 102.

question: Friedrich Hayek's Prices and Production (1931) laid out the most developed version of Austrian Business Cycle Theory. The theory pictures the structure of production as a multi-stage process. When the central bank lowers interest rates below the natural rate, what does Hayek say happens to that structure?
answer: Capital flows into longer, more roundabout projects that look profitable at the artificial low rate — they are revealed as malinvestments once rates normalize
choices: Capital flows into longer, more roundabout projects that look profitable at the artificial low rate — they are revealed as malinvestments once rates normalize
Capital flows uniformly into all sectors — Hayek argued lower rates produce balanced growth without distorting the structure of production at any horizon
Capital leaves the economy entirely — Hayek argued lower rates cause capital flight to foreign markets where rates remain higher under fixed exchange
Capital is destroyed by inflation — Hayek argued lower rates immediately raise consumer prices without affecting the time structure of investment at all
context: Hayek's triangular diagram of the time-structure of production became a famous Austrian teaching device. The theory predicted that artificially-low rates would later require a corrective recession to liquidate malinvestments. The 2008 housing collapse is the canonical modern application.

question: ABCT wasn't invented by Hayek alone — it grew out of Mises's 1912 Theory of Money and Credit and Knut Wicksell's work on the 'natural' interest rate. Wicksell distinguished the natural rate (where savings equal investment) from the market rate set by banks. When the market rate falls below the natural rate, ABCT predicts what?
answer: An unsustainable boom — businesses borrow at the artificially low rate for projects savings wouldn't have supported, and the boom must end when reality reasserts itself
choices: An unsustainable boom — businesses borrow at the artificially low rate for projects savings wouldn't have supported, and the boom must end when reality reasserts itself
A sustainable expansion — any gap between natural and market rates produces permanent economic growth without any later correction
Immediate deflation — any gap between natural and market rates causes prices to fall faster than wages, choking off all credit at once
No effect at all — banks cannot influence the natural rate of interest, so deviations between rates have no measurable consequences
context: Wicksell's 1898 Interest and Prices laid out the natural-vs-market rate distinction. Mises integrated it into a full theory of money and credit cycles. Hayek made the time-structure of production explicit. The lineage runs Wicksell → Mises → Hayek → modern Austrians.

question: Frédéric Bastiat — French parliamentary deputy, classical-liberal pamphleteer — published The Law in June 1850, weeks before he died of throat cancer in Rome at age 49. The pamphlet's central question: what is law for? Bastiat answered with his characteristic clarity: it has one legitimate function. What is it?
answer: Defending the natural rights to person, liberty, and property — anything beyond that turns law into 'legal plunder' on behalf of one group at another's expense
choices: Defending the natural rights to person, liberty, and property — anything beyond that turns law into 'legal plunder' on behalf of one group at another's expense
Promoting equality of outcomes — Bastiat argued law should redistribute wealth from rich to poor as its primary justified purpose for any modern society
Building infrastructure and public goods — Bastiat argued law's main purpose is funding roads, bridges, and schools from compulsory taxation revenues
Maintaining social hierarchy — Bastiat argued law's main purpose is preserving aristocratic privilege against democratic encroachments by any means available
context: The Law is a short read (about 60 pages) and is still in print. Bastiat's phrase 'legal plunder' refers to law being used to take from one group and give to another — what later writers call rent-seeking. His broader work was the founding French statement of free-trade and seen-vs-unseen economic reasoning.

question: Frédéric Bastiat published 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen' in July 1850 — the last essay he would write before his death months later. The pamphlet introduced the core method of folk economic reasoning. What's the method, in Bastiat's own framing?
answer: Trace every economic action not just to its visible immediate effect — but also to all the unseen secondary effects on parties not directly involved
choices: Trace every economic action not just to its visible immediate effect — but also to all the unseen secondary effects on parties not directly involved
Calculate the aggregate change in GDP — every economic action either raises or lowers national output in a manner economists can measure with precision
Identify the moral character of each actor — Bastiat argued economic outcomes follow primarily from the virtue or vice of individual participants in trade
Apply the labor theory of value — Bastiat argued that the value of any good comes from the hours of labor required to produce it under the prevailing technology
context: The essay contains the broken-window fallacy and many other Bastiat illustrations — the candle-makers' petition against the sun's unfair competition, the negative railway, the conscription debate. The method is the foundational lesson of the Austrian-leaning popular-economics tradition. Henry Hazlitt's Economics in One Lesson (1946) is the great mid-20th-century restatement.

question: Bastiat's most famous illustration of seen-vs-unseen appears at the start of 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen' (1850). A shopkeeper's careless son breaks a window. A crowd concludes the accident helps the economy — the glazier gets work, his family eats, the chain continues. Where's the missing piece?
answer: The shopkeeper would have spent the same money on shoes or a coat — those purchases didn't happen, and the unseen tailor or shoemaker is poorer for the broken window
choices: The shopkeeper would have spent the same money on shoes or a coat — those purchases didn't happen, and the unseen tailor or shoemaker is poorer for the broken window
The glazier should have charged less for the repair — Bastiat argued fair pricing is the missing piece in voluntary exchanges between strangers
The boy should have been punished — Bastiat's argument was about individual moral responsibility rather than economic reasoning
The shopkeeper should have insured the window — Bastiat argued risk pooling is the missing piece in folk economic reasoning
context: The broken-window fallacy is the canonical Austrian-leaning teaching example. It applies to wartime production ('the war is good for the economy'), natural disasters ('rebuilding stimulates demand'), and Keynesian stimulus ('government spending creates jobs'). In each case, the seen benefit is real — but the unseen cost is larger.

question: Frédéric Bastiat published a satirical 'Petition of the Candlemakers' in his 1845 Economic Sophisms — a fake petition to the French Chamber of Deputies on behalf of candle, lantern, and lampmakers. The petition demanded protection against an unfair foreign competitor undercutting their prices. Who was the foreign competitor?
answer: The Sun — Bastiat used the absurd target to expose the same protectionist logic French manufacturers were using against actual foreign goods
choices: The Sun — Bastiat used the absurd target to expose the same protectionist logic French manufacturers were using against actual foreign goods
Belgian candlemakers — the satire was a literal protest against Belgium's flooding of the French market with cheaper tallow candles in 1845
Whale-oil importers — the satire was a literal protest against American whale-oil exports undercutting French lighting suppliers in the 1840s
Electric lighting — the satire was a literal protest against Edison's incandescent bulb, which was being introduced into Paris in the mid-1840s
context: The petition demanded the government order all windows, skylights, shutters, and curtains closed during daylight hours — to protect the candlemakers from solar competition. Bastiat's satire remains one of the great anti-protectionist texts in any language. Edison's bulb came decades later (1879).

question: Lew Rockwell, Burton Blumert, and Murray Rothbard founded the Ludwig von Mises Institute in October 1982 — soon settling at Auburn University in Alabama. Margit von Mises (Mises's widow) gave her blessing and provided his library and personal papers. What was the Institute meant to do?
answer: Preserve and extend Austrian economics outside the mainstream universities — keeping the tradition alive through publications, conferences, and student programs
choices: Preserve and extend Austrian economics outside the mainstream universities — keeping the tradition alive through publications, conferences, and student programs
Coordinate Austrian-school job placements in the Federal Reserve — Rockwell aimed to staff the central bank with sound-money advocates from his Institute
Lobby Congress for monetary reform legislation — the Institute was set up as a 501(c)(4) with a specific bill on the table at founding
Run an investment fund for Austrian-aligned wealthy donors — Rothbard aimed to combine academic work with private wealth management services
context: The Mises Institute's annual Mises University at Auburn has trained generations of scholars. Hans-Hermann Hoppe, Joseph Salerno, Guido Hülsmann, and many others have been associated with it. Mises.org has become one of the most widely-read economics websites. Rockwell remains chairman; Jeff Deist later served as president.

question: Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom appeared in March 1944 — published in Britain with US release that fall. The book was dedicated 'to the socialists of all parties' and aimed at British and American audiences sympathetic to wartime central planning. What was Hayek's central warning?
answer: Comprehensive economic planning erodes the conditions for political liberty — planning a whole economy requires power that eventually substitutes for the rule of law itself
choices: Comprehensive economic planning erodes the conditions for political liberty — planning a whole economy requires power that eventually substitutes for the rule of law itself
Wartime planning was justified — Hayek argued the British and US war economies should remain centrally planned indefinitely as a model for peace
Free markets cause fascism — Hayek argued that capitalism leads to Nazi-style totalitarianism over time across all industrialized economies
Democracy is incompatible with markets — Hayek argued voters should be replaced by technical experts in setting national economic priorities
context: Reader's Digest published an abridgement in April 1945 that reached millions. The University of Chicago Press edition sold steadily through the postwar decades. The book made Hayek famous outside professional economics — and angered Keynesian and socialist contemporaries. The 1989-91 collapse of the Eastern bloc retroactively underscored its argument.

question: Carl Menger published Grundsätze der Volkswirtschaftslehre — Principles of Economics — in Vienna in 1871. The book launched what would become the Austrian school. The same year, Jevons in Manchester and Walras in Lausanne independently published similar ideas — together known as the 'marginal revolution.' What was Menger's central move?
answer: Grounding value in subjective marginal utility — what you'd give up to get one more unit — rather than in objective labor input or cost of production
choices: Grounding value in subjective marginal utility — what you'd give up to get one more unit — rather than in objective labor input or cost of production
Grounding value in total social labor hours — Menger built on Ricardo's labor theory and refined it for industrial-era Austrian textile manufacturing
Grounding value in the gold standard — Menger argued that all economic value must be expressed in fixed monetary terms backed by precious metals
Grounding value in mathematical equilibrium models — Menger founded the Austrian school by introducing calculus into Vienna university economics
context: Menger later tutored Crown Prince Rudolf of Austria. His Principles is the foundational Austrian text — short, clear, focused on the subjective theory of value. Bohm-Bawerk and Wieser were among his early followers. The marginalist revolution displaced the classical (Smith, Ricardo, Marx) labor theory of value.

question: Eugen von Bohm-Bawerk — Menger's student, three-time Finance Minister of Austria-Hungary — published his three-volume Capital and Interest between 1884 and 1889. The work is best known for one negative argument: a sustained demolition of every previous theory of interest. What was his positive theory?
answer: Interest reflects 'time preference' — people generally value present goods over future goods, and the rate of interest is the market price of that preference
choices: Interest reflects 'time preference' — people generally value present goods over future goods, and the rate of interest is the market price of that preference
Interest reflects unequal bargaining power — Bohm-Bawerk argued lenders extract a usurious markup from borrowers due to monopolistic concentration of capital
Interest reflects the productivity of capital alone — Bohm-Bawerk argued interest equals exactly the marginal product of physical capital with no other input
Interest reflects state monopoly — Bohm-Bawerk argued the rate of interest is set entirely by central authorities and cannot exist in genuinely free markets
context: Bohm-Bawerk's most famous chapter — 'The Marxian Exploitation Theory' — is a long refutation of Marx's labor theory of value. The volumes are dense going but foundational for Austrian capital theory. Mises and Hayek both drew on Bohm-Bawerk in their later business-cycle work.

question: Hayek's 1945 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' opened with a memorable example. He asked the reader to imagine a sudden tin shortage. Producers using tin in any product need to economize on it. Yet no central authority broadcasts 'tin is scarce — economize.' How does the adjustment happen?
answer: The price of tin rises — and every user, without knowing the cause, responds by economizing — dispersed users coordinate through prices alone, never needing the underlying story
choices: The price of tin rises — and every user, without knowing the cause, responds by economizing — dispersed users coordinate through prices alone, never needing the underlying story
The Bureau of Mines issues a daily bulletin — Hayek argued government information agencies are essential for coordinating responses to commodity shortages
Producers form a cartel meeting — Hayek argued industry self-regulation through formal coordination meetings is how shortages get managed in practice
The adjustment never happens — Hayek argued shortages cannot be resolved by markets and always require central rationing to allocate scarce supplies
context: Hayek's tin example is one of the great teaching moments in 20th-century economics. The price encodes information no individual possesses. The argument is the practical extension of Mises's 1920 calculation insight: prices ARE the calculation, and you can't have one without the other.

question: Richard Cantillon — Irish-French banker who knew John Law and made a fortune in Law's Mississippi Bubble before it collapsed — wrote his Essai sur la Nature du Commerce en Général in the late 1720s (published 1755). He observed that when new money enters an economy, prices don't all rise at once. What did he see?
answer: First holders of new money buy at old prices — by the time money has rippled out, prices have risen — so early recipients gain at the expense of late ones
choices: First holders of new money buy at old prices — by the time money has rippled out, prices have risen — so early recipients gain at the expense of late ones
Money expansion is neutral in every respect — Cantillon argued all prices rise instantaneously across the economy the day new money appears
Money expansion benefits late recipients first — Cantillon argued wages adjust before any other prices, so workers gain before businesses raise goods
Money expansion has no effect on prices — Cantillon argued the velocity of circulation always compensates for any change in money supply
context: Cantillon's insight — the 'Cantillon effect' — was rediscovered by Mises and refined by modern Austrians as the explanation for why monetary inflation is regressive even when CPI looks modest. New money rewards proximity to issuance: banks, government contractors, asset holders gain; wage earners and savers lose.

question: Ronald Coase published 'The Nature of the Firm' in Economica in 1937 — he was 26, having developed the argument as an undergrad at LSE. The paper asked a question every textbook ignored: if markets coordinate so well, why do firms exist at all? Why not have every transaction happen through individual contracts?
answer: Markets have transaction costs — searching, negotiating, contracting — and firms exist because organizing some activities internally is cheaper than running everything through market exchange
choices: Markets have transaction costs — searching, negotiating, contracting — and firms exist because organizing some activities internally is cheaper than running everything through market exchange
Firms exist purely for legal protection — Coase argued limited liability is the only reason corporations exist instead of partnerships and proprietorships
Firms exist to capture monopoly profits — Coase argued the only reason firms grow beyond a single proprietor is to suppress competition and raise prices
Firms exist by government decree — Coase argued the corporate form is a state creation with no organic economic rationale at all
context: Coase's paper sat in the literature for decades before being widely appreciated. His later work (1960, on social cost) extended the transaction-cost insight to the institutional structure of property rights. Both papers together earned him the 1991 Nobel. Oliver Williamson developed the transaction-cost framework further; he won the 2009 Nobel.

question: Thomas Sowell published Knowledge and Decisions in 1980 — a book that won the Law and Economics Center's Prize and gave his career a substantial boost. The book applied Hayek's 1945 knowledge-problem insight to a broad range of institutional questions. What was the recurring framework?
answer: Different institutions process different kinds of knowledge — markets handle dispersed local data well, courts handle precedent well, governments handle neither efficiently across most domains
choices: Different institutions process different kinds of knowledge — markets handle dispersed local data well, courts handle precedent well, governments handle neither efficiently across most domains
All institutions process knowledge identically — Sowell argued government, markets, and courts all use the same information-processing logic in equilibrium
Markets cannot process knowledge — Sowell argued only central planning agencies can efficiently aggregate information across an entire economy
Knowledge is irrelevant to institutional design — Sowell argued institutional choices are made on moral grounds alone, with no efficiency considerations involved
context: Sowell's book applied the framework to busing, affirmative action, antitrust, financial regulation, and other policy questions. His 1996 book Migrations and Cultures and 1998 Conquests and Cultures extended the analysis to international comparative cases. Knowledge and Decisions remains one of his most cited works.

question: Thomas Sowell's Basic Economics first appeared in 2000 — a long-form introduction to economic reasoning aimed at general readers, with no graphs, equations, or technical jargon. The book has run through five editions, the latest in 2014, each substantially expanded. What's its distinctive teaching method?
answer: Real-world examples from many countries and eras — drawing economic lessons from concrete cases instead of abstract models or mathematical formulations
choices: Real-world examples from many countries and eras — drawing economic lessons from concrete cases instead of abstract models or mathematical formulations
Long mathematical derivations from first principles — Sowell aimed Basic Economics at undergraduate seniors with calculus and statistics background
Survey of current macroeconomic data — Sowell organized the book around updated GDP and inflation statistics rather than historical or international examples
A defense of Keynesian fiscal policy — Sowell wrote the book to popularize aggregate-demand management for the millennial-era general public
context: Sowell's accessible style has made Basic Economics one of the best-selling popular economics books of the 21st century. His Applied Economics (2003) is a companion volume on policy applications. Henry Hazlitt's 1946 Economics in One Lesson is the closest predecessor in spirit and method.

question: Murray Rothbard published For a New Liberty in 1973 — a manifesto for the modern libertarian movement, written for a popular audience. The book sketched a society where every government function — police, courts, roads, defense — was privately produced rather than state-monopolized. What's the framework called?
answer: Anarcho-capitalism — voluntary private institutions, including private courts and protection agencies, replacing every coercive function of the state
choices: Anarcho-capitalism — voluntary private institutions, including private courts and protection agencies, replacing every coercive function of the state
Constitutional minarchism — Rothbard argued for a small night-watchman state confined to police, courts, and defense as the only legitimate functions
Social democracy — Rothbard's 1973 book represented his pivot toward European-style welfare-state economics for the remainder of his career
Distributism — Rothbard's 1973 book endorsed the Catholic-traditionalist program of widely-held small property ownership and guild structures
context: Rothbard's framework — coined by him 'anarcho-capitalism' — drew on the natural-rights tradition (Locke, Bastiat, Spooner, Tucker) and Austrian economics. Critics across the spectrum have pushed hard cases. Modern figures including Hans-Hermann Hoppe and David Friedman have continued the analysis along different lines.

question: George Stigler — University of Chicago, 1982 Nobel laureate — published 'The Theory of Economic Regulation' in 1971. The paper turned a folk observation into a formal economic theory: regulatory agencies often end up serving the industries they regulate, not the public. What was Stigler's mechanism?
answer: Regulators face concentrated industry interests with high stakes — and diffuse public interests with low individual stakes — so industry tends to dominate the political-economic process
choices: Regulators face concentrated industry interests with high stakes — and diffuse public interests with low individual stakes — so industry tends to dominate the political-economic process
Regulators are inherently corrupt — Stigler argued that any regulatory body must eventually take bribes from the industry it oversees, regardless of design
Regulators serve the public well by definition — Stigler argued that capture is a myth and his paper aimed to defend the existing regulatory state
Regulators are necessary for markets — Stigler argued in this paper that markets without regulation always collapse into monopoly within a decade
context: Stigler's paper gave rigorous form to what Marver Bernstein and others had observed earlier. Combined with public choice (Buchanan, Tullock) and rent-seeking (Tullock 1967, Krueger 1974), the recognition reshaped how economists think about regulation. The 'revolving door' between regulators and the industries they regulate is one common visible manifestation.

question: Friedrich Hayek published The Constitution of Liberty in 1960 — a 500-page systematic treatise on political philosophy. Hayek considered it his best book. The first part traced the historical development of the idea of liberty under law. What did the book argue is the precondition for liberty?
answer: General, abstract, prospective rules applying equally to all — not specific commands or targeted favors handed out by lawmakers to particular groups
choices: General, abstract, prospective rules applying equally to all — not specific commands or targeted favors handed out by lawmakers to particular groups
Direct democracy with universal participation — Hayek argued every citizen must vote on every law for the legal order to be considered legitimate
A strong, unconstrained executive — Hayek argued only an unchecked head of state can defend liberty against legislative encroachment in modern conditions
Constitutional monarchy — Hayek argued in this book that hereditary monarchs are the most reliable defenders of liberty against democratic pressures
context: Margaret Thatcher famously slammed The Constitution of Liberty on a table during a 1975 meeting, telling colleagues 'this is what we believe.' Hayek's Law, Legislation and Liberty (1973-79, three volumes) extended the framework. The Constitution of Liberty's appendix 'Why I Am Not a Conservative' clarified Hayek's classical-liberal distinction from Anglo-American conservatism.

question: Thomas Sowell published Discrimination and Disparities in 2018, with a second edition in 2019. The book attacked a widespread assumption in policy discussion: that group differences in outcomes must be explained by either discrimination or genetics. What's Sowell's central argument?
answer: Group disparities reflect many causes — culture, geography, demographics, age, family structure, choices — and treating every disparity as evidence of discrimination misreads the data
choices: Group disparities reflect many causes — culture, geography, demographics, age, family structure, choices — and treating every disparity as evidence of discrimination misreads the data
Group disparities are entirely caused by current discrimination — Sowell argued in this book that no other causes contribute to observable income or wealth gaps
Group disparities are entirely caused by genetic differences — Sowell endorsed a biological-essentialist framework in this 2018 book on social policy
Group disparities are entirely random — Sowell argued in this book that all observed differences between groups are statistical noise without underlying causes
context: Sowell drew on his earlier comparative-cultures research (Migrations and Cultures, Conquests and Cultures, Race and Culture) to show how varied the causes of group disparities are in international historical data. The book is sharply critical of the disparate-impact framework underlying much US civil-rights litigation.

question: Frédéric Bastiat published 'The State' (L'État) in September 1848 — months after the February Revolution had brought a new French government promising prosperity through state action. Bastiat's satirical definition has become one of the most-quoted lines in classical-liberal literature. How did he define the state?
answer: The state is the great fiction by which everyone endeavors to live at the expense of everyone else — a vivid summary of redistributive politics in one sentence
choices: The state is the great fiction by which everyone endeavors to live at the expense of everyone else — a vivid summary of redistributive politics in one sentence
The state is the highest expression of human cooperation — Bastiat used this 1848 pamphlet to defend the new French Second Republic against critics
The state is the necessary partner of the market — Bastiat argued in this 1848 pamphlet that public and private spheres must merge to produce prosperity
The state is identical to civil society — Bastiat argued in this 1848 pamphlet that no analytical distinction can be drawn between the two domains
context: Bastiat was a deputy in the Constituent Assembly of the French Second Republic at the time of writing. He sat with the moderates, defending free trade and limited government against both the socialist left and the protectionist right. He died December 24, 1850, in Rome, of throat cancer, at age 49.

question: Henry Hazlitt — Wall Street Journal financial editor, New York Times editorial-board member — published Economics in One Lesson in 1946. The book became one of the best-selling economics primers ever written. Hazlitt drew explicitly on Bastiat's seen-vs-unseen framework. What was the 'one lesson'?
answer: Trace every economic policy not just to its immediate effects on one group — but to its longer-term effects on all groups, including effects that aren't immediately visible
choices: Trace every economic policy not just to its immediate effects on one group — but to its longer-term effects on all groups, including effects that aren't immediately visible
Maximize aggregate GDP growth — Hazlitt argued the one lesson of economics is to support every policy that raises measured national output in the short term
Apply mathematical models rigorously — Hazlitt argued the one lesson of economics is the necessity of formal training in calculus and statistics for policy work
Defer to expert opinion — Hazlitt argued the one lesson of economics is that ordinary citizens should never form views on policy without specialist credentials
context: Hazlitt updated and re-released the book in 1979. It remains in print and has been translated into many languages. Hazlitt also wrote The Failure of the 'New Economics' (1959), a chapter-by-chapter critique of Keynes's General Theory. He was a friend of Mises and an officer of the Foundation for Economic Education.

question: Ludwig von Mises published Liberalismus in Vienna in 1927 — a short systematic statement of classical-liberal political theory (the English translation is Liberalism: In the Classical Tradition). Mises was 46, at the height of his Vienna years. What did the book argue is the moral foundation of the free society?
answer: Private property in the means of production — the institutional precondition for peace, prosperity, and individual liberty across history
choices: Private property in the means of production — the institutional precondition for peace, prosperity, and individual liberty across history
Democratic majority rule — Mises argued universal suffrage is the foundation of the free society in this 1927 statement of his political views
Equality of outcomes — Mises argued material equality between citizens is the foundation of a peaceful and free political community of any kind
A strong central state — Mises argued the rule of law requires concentrated government authority to override local custom and tradition firmly
context: Mises's Liberalism remains a clear statement of the classical-liberal position. He argued private property in capital goods is what distinguishes the modern free society from all earlier forms of social organization. The book preceded his more comprehensive Human Action (1949) by 22 years and Hayek's Constitution of Liberty (1960) by 33 years.

question: Hans-Hermann Hoppe — born 1949 in West Germany, trained as a Habermas student before his Austrian conversion — moved to the University of Nevada, Las Vegas in 1986 at Rothbard's invitation. After Rothbard's death in 1995 Hoppe became one of the most prominent figures in the Austrian-libertarian tradition. What's his characteristic methodological move?
answer: Argumentation ethics — deriving the legitimacy of property rights from the very act of arguing, claiming the principle is self-refuting to deny
choices: Argumentation ethics — deriving the legitimacy of property rights from the very act of arguing, claiming the principle is self-refuting to deny
Statistical hypothesis testing — Hoppe argued the empirical-data approach is the only valid foundation for any economic or ethical analysis
Game-theoretic equilibrium — Hoppe argued game theory derivations are the only valid foundation for political and economic claims about human action
Behavioral psychology surveys — Hoppe argued opinion polling provides the most reliable empirical basis for ethical and political conclusions in modern conditions
context: Hoppe's Democracy: The God That Failed (2001) and A Theory of Socialism and Capitalism (1989) are his best-known works. The annual Property and Freedom Society conference (founded 2006, Bodrum, Turkey) is his vehicle. His provocative positions on democracy and immigration generated controversy even within libertarian circles.

question: Joseph Salerno — Pace University professor, Mises Institute Academic Vice President — is a leading contemporary Austrian monetary theorist. His Money, Sound and Unsound (2010) collected decades of work on the calculation debate, monetary equilibrium, and free banking. What's his characteristic claim about the calculation debate?
answer: The Mises argument was about RATIONAL CALCULATION — not just any efficiency claim — and most modern restatements miss what Mises actually argued in 1920
choices: The Mises argument was about RATIONAL CALCULATION — not just any efficiency claim — and most modern restatements miss what Mises actually argued in 1920
The Mises argument was entirely empirical — Salerno argued the calculation debate hinges on statistical comparisons of Soviet vs US GDP growth in the 20th century
The Mises argument has been refuted — Salerno conceded in 2010 that market socialists like Oskar Lange had the better of the calculation debate
The Mises argument was about voter behavior — Salerno argued the 1920 paper was concerned with electoral choice rather than economic organization
context: Salerno has done careful textual work on Mises's calculation argument and its evolution. His distinction between 'calculation' (using actual money prices) and broader 'computability' arguments has been influential in Austrian methodological discussion. He also edits the Quarterly Journal of Austrian Economics.

question: Peter Boettke — George Mason University, director of the F.A. Hayek Program — is a leading mainstream-engaged Austrian economist. His Why Perestroika Failed (1993) used Mises and Hayek to predict the trajectory of post-Soviet economic reform. What did Boettke get right that consensus economists missed?
answer: Without prior institutional change — property rights, rule of law — opening the Soviet economy to markets would produce chaos, not the smooth transition Western advisors expected
choices: Without prior institutional change — property rights, rule of law — opening the Soviet economy to markets would produce chaos, not the smooth transition Western advisors expected
The Soviet economy would smoothly transition to markets — Boettke argued in 1993 that institutional details didn't matter once price controls were removed
The Soviet economy was fundamentally sound — Boettke argued in 1993 that no reform was needed and central planning would survive intact
Perestroika would restore the Soviet Union — Boettke argued in 1993 that Gorbachev's reforms would strengthen rather than undermine the central state
context: Boettke's GMU Hayek Program has trained a generation of Austrian-influenced scholars working in academic economics. His Living Economics (2012) and The Struggle for a Better World (2021) extend the analysis. He is one of the most influential figures in the modern Austrian revival within academic economics.

question: Thomas Sowell published The Vision of the Anointed in 1995 — a critique of a recurring pattern in 20th-century policy discussion. Sowell identified a vision — held by people he called 'the anointed' — that explained why the same kinds of policies kept being proposed regardless of past failures. What's the vision?
answer: Society's problems result from leaders' wrong ideas — and could be solved if the right people (intellectuals, experts, judges) had the power to impose better ideas top-down
choices: Society's problems result from leaders' wrong ideas — and could be solved if the right people (intellectuals, experts, judges) had the power to impose better ideas top-down
Society's problems are inevitable and unsolvable — Sowell argued the anointed believe no government policy can ever produce any meaningful improvement at all
Society's problems can only be solved by markets — Sowell argued the anointed are libertarian intellectuals proposing universal deregulation as the cure
Society's problems are caused by genetics — Sowell argued the anointed are biological essentialists who attribute outcomes to inherited traits
context: Sowell contrasted 'the vision of the anointed' with what he called 'the tragic vision' — the older view (Smith, Burke, Hayek, Sowell himself) that knowledge is dispersed, institutions evolve, and trade-offs are unavoidable. The book is a sequel to Sowell's A Conflict of Visions (1987). Both remain widely cited.

question: Milton Friedman won the 1976 Nobel in Economics for his work in consumption analysis, monetary history and theory, and stabilization policy. Friedman, at Chicago, had been the leading academic voice against postwar Keynesian orthodoxy for two decades. What was his core monetary claim?
answer: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon — caused by the central bank printing money faster than real output grows, not by 'cost-push' or 'demand-pull' factors
choices: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon — caused by the central bank printing money faster than real output grows, not by 'cost-push' or 'demand-pull' factors
Inflation is always a fiscal phenomenon — Friedman argued government deficits directly cause inflation independent of any monetary expansion
Inflation is caused by trade unions — Friedman argued in his Nobel work that wage-push from collective bargaining is the sole driver of price increases
Inflation is caused by oil prices — Friedman argued the 1970s inflation was entirely due to OPEC supply shocks with no monetary component
context: Friedman's Nobel citation specifically honored his consumption analysis (the permanent-income hypothesis), monetary history (with Schwartz), and stabilization-policy work. The 'quantity theory of money' he revived is older than monetarism, but his empirical work and policy advocacy gave it dominant influence by the late 1970s.

question: Mises's NYU Thursday-night seminar (1948-1969) drew a remarkable group of attendees over its 21-year run. Murray Rothbard was the best known. Israel Kirzner — later author of Competition and Entrepreneurship (1973) — was another. Hans Sennholz, George Reisman, Ralph Raico, Louis Spadaro. Why was the seminar significant institutionally?
answer: It was the only place in postwar US academia where Austrian economics was taught seriously — producing nearly every later Austrian scholar in the United States
choices: It was the only place in postwar US academia where Austrian economics was taught seriously — producing nearly every later Austrian scholar in the United States
It was a major training ground for Federal Reserve economists — Mises's students dominated the Fed's research division throughout the 1960s and 1970s
It was a Communist Party USA front — Mises had retained his early socialist sympathies and used the seminar to recruit graduate students to the party
It was a major training ground for Wall Street investment bankers — Mises's students dominated the asset-management industry in the postwar period
context: Israel Kirzner's later work on the entrepreneur as discovery-process is one of the major postwar Austrian contributions. Kirzner remained at NYU into the 21st century. The seminar's institutional legacy outlived Mises by decades, with many participants moving into academic posts at smaller universities or into research institutes.

question: The quantity theory of money — revived by Milton Friedman and his Chicago colleagues — is often summarized in the equation MV = PT. Money supply times velocity equals price level times transactions volume. Friedman's empirical work argued one variable was usefully stable in the medium run. Which one?
answer: Velocity is reasonably stable — so changes in money supply translate fairly predictably into changes in nominal output and prices, vindicating monetary policy as the dominant factor
choices: Velocity is reasonably stable — so changes in money supply translate fairly predictably into changes in nominal output and prices, vindicating monetary policy as the dominant factor
Money supply is stable — Friedman argued central banks had little control over M2 and fiscal policy was therefore the dominant stabilization lever
Price level is stable — Friedman argued inflation is essentially impossible in any modern fiat-money economy in this framework
Transactions volume is stable — Friedman argued real GDP cannot change in the short run and monetary expansion only affects velocity
context: Friedman's velocity claim was empirically fragile by the 1980s (velocity became less stable than monetarism required for tight money-supply targeting). Central banks moved away from M-aggregate targeting toward inflation targeting and interest-rate rules. The Austrian and monetarist diagnoses of fiat money's problems differ, but both recognize central-bank monetary expansion as the proximate cause of inflation.

question: Israel Kirzner — Mises's most academically successful direct student, longtime NYU professor — published Competition and Entrepreneurship in 1973. The book offered a distinctive Austrian account of how markets coordinate. What's the role of the entrepreneur in Kirzner's framework?
answer: Alertness to opportunities — entrepreneurs notice profitable arbitrage opportunities others have missed, and their action moves the market toward equilibrium one step at a time
choices: Alertness to opportunities — entrepreneurs notice profitable arbitrage opportunities others have missed, and their action moves the market toward equilibrium one step at a time
Random behavior under uncertainty — Kirzner argued entrepreneurs are gamblers whose actions average out to nothing in aggregate over long enough time horizons
Government-licensed innovators — Kirzner argued the entrepreneurs of his theory are state-credentialed actors operating under strict licensing regimes
Capital owners with no specific function — Kirzner argued the term 'entrepreneur' simply means anyone who happens to own capital regardless of action
context: Kirzner's framework differs from Schumpeter's 'creative destruction' view of the entrepreneur as a disruptive innovator. Kirzner's entrepreneur is more modest — alert to small price discrepancies — but cumulatively responsible for market coordination. Kirzner died March 5, 2025, at age 95, having taught and written for decades.

question: Roger Garrison — longtime Auburn University professor — published Time and Money: The Macroeconomics of Capital Structure in 2001. The book is the most systematic modern statement of Austrian Business Cycle Theory, using graphical tools that compare to standard macro textbooks. What's the book's distinctive contribution?
answer: Putting Hayek's time-structure of production into a teachable graphical framework — showing how monetary expansion distorts capital structure in ways aggregate models hide
choices: Putting Hayek's time-structure of production into a teachable graphical framework — showing how monetary expansion distorts capital structure in ways aggregate models hide
Refuting Hayek's business cycle theory — Garrison argued ABCT is incompatible with modern monetary economics and proposed replacing it with monetarism
Defending Keynesian fiscal multipliers — Garrison argued in 2001 that aggregate demand management is the appropriate macroeconomic policy framework
Endorsing MMT principles — Garrison argued government deficits are constrained only by inflation and produced this book to popularize MMT
context: Garrison's book brought the Hayekian capital-structure framework into engagement with mainstream macro textbooks. Time and Money has been cited extensively in the 2008-and-after revival of interest in Austrian cycle theory. Garrison retired from Auburn after a long teaching career; the Mises Institute archived his lectures.

question: Anthony Downs — Stanford-trained economist — published An Economic Theory of Democracy in 1957. The book made a startling rational-choice claim about voter behavior in modern democracies. What did Downs predict an individual voter would do, given the tiny probability of casting the decisive ballot?
answer: Stay rationally ignorant — gathering detailed political information has high cost and almost zero benefit at the margin, so most voters never investigate carefully
choices: Stay rationally ignorant — gathering detailed political information has high cost and almost zero benefit at the margin, so most voters never investigate carefully
Become rationally well-informed — Downs argued democratic competition produces voters who research candidates as thoroughly as they research consumer goods
Abstain entirely from politics — Downs predicted turnout would fall to under 5 percent in mature democracies as rational-ignorance effects accumulated
Coordinate with interest groups — Downs predicted voters would always follow union or church leaders' directives without ever forming independent views
context: Rational ignorance is one of the great public-choice insights. It explains why concentrated interests (lobbyists with high per-capita stakes) tend to dominate dispersed interests (taxpayers with low per-capita stakes). Combined with Tullock's rent-seeking and Buchanan's constitutional analysis, the picture of democratic politics is sobering — and very different from the textbook ideal.

question: Anne Krueger — later Chief Economist at the World Bank — published 'The Political Economy of the Rent-Seeking Society' in the American Economic Review in 1974. Krueger's paper extended Tullock's 1967 analysis with empirical estimates from India and Turkey. What did she contribute that Tullock's earlier paper hadn't?
answer: The name 'rent-seeking' itself — and quantitative estimates of how much of GDP is wasted competing for political privilege in developing economies with extensive licensing systems
choices: The name 'rent-seeking' itself — and quantitative estimates of how much of GDP is wasted competing for political privilege in developing economies with extensive licensing systems
A mathematical proof that rent-seeking does not exist — Krueger's 1974 paper refuted Tullock's earlier work using formal optimization techniques
A defense of the rent-seeking equilibrium — Krueger argued in 1974 that competition for political privilege produces optimal outcomes under most conditions
