answer: Bitcoin's base layer settles roughly 7 transactions per second to maintain decentralization; Lightning scales payments without compromising the base layer's monetary properties
choices: Bitcoin's base layer settles roughly 7 transactions per second to maintain decentralization; Lightning scales payments without compromising the base layer's monetary properties
Lightning replaces Bitcoin entirely with a new proof-of-stake consensus mechanism and is intended to make the original Bitcoin protocol obsolete by the end of the decade
Lightning is operated by a centralized company in Switzerland that holds custody of all funds in payment channels, similar to traditional payment processors like Visa and Mastercard
Lightning was abandoned in 2020 after failing to attract significant user adoption and is no longer an active part of the Bitcoin ecosystem despite occasional references in technical papers
context: Lightning capacity grew from ~100 BTC in 2019 to over 5,000 BTC by 2024. El Salvador's Chivo wallet uses Lightning for daily transactions. The Cash App and Strike integrations brought Lightning to mainstream US users. The 'scaling debate' of 2015-17 (Bitcoin Cash hard fork) was effectively settled by Lightning's success.

question: Bitcoin's 'block size war' of 2015-2017 pitted larger-block advocates (Bitcoin Cash, Bitcoin Unlimited) against off-chain scalers via Segregated Witness (SegWit) and Lightning. August 2017 SegWit activated via miner signaling without a hard fork. The November 2017 'Segwit2X' attempt to force a 2MB hard fork was abandoned. What was the disagreement?
answer: Whether to scale Bitcoin by raising on-chain capacity (sacrificing some decentralization) or by building payment layers on top while keeping the base layer small and verifiable
choices: Whether to scale Bitcoin by raising on-chain capacity (sacrificing some decentralization) or by building payment layers on top while keeping the base layer small and verifiable
Whether Bitcoin should adopt the Ethereum smart-contract framework as its primary use case or remain limited to simple monetary transfers as Satoshi originally intended in 2008
Whether Bitcoin should transition to proof-of-stake consensus or remain on proof-of-work, with the small-block faction representing proof-of-stake advocates against the larger group
Whether Bitcoin should be administered by a central foundation or remain decentralized, with the large-block faction supporting a new Bitcoin Foundation board to govern protocol
context: Roger Ver, Jihan Wu, and others led the Bitcoin Cash fork in August 2017. By 2024, BCH had a tiny fraction of Bitcoin's market cap and adoption. The small-block side's bet on Lightning + base-layer decentralization is now considered vindicated by market action.

question: The Aldrich Plan drafted at Jekyll Island in November 1910 by Senator Nelson Aldrich and Wall Street bankers was rejected by Congress in 1912 as too obviously a banker-run scheme. Carter Glass and Robert Owen modified it: same regional-reserve-bank architecture, with a federal Board of Governors overlaid for political cover. The Federal Reserve Act passed December 23, 1913. What changed substantively?
answer: Glass-Owen kept the Aldrich Plan's bank-friendly regional structure and added a thin layer of presidential appointment, so the underlying private-bank coordination survived intact
choices: Glass-Owen kept the Aldrich Plan's bank-friendly regional structure and added a thin layer of presidential appointment, so the underlying private-bank coordination survived intact
Glass-Owen eliminated all private-bank involvement in the Federal Reserve System, making the Fed a fully public agency under direct Treasury Department control from 1913 onward
The Aldrich Plan and Glass-Owen were completely different proposals with no architectural similarity, and the eventual Federal Reserve owed nothing to the Jekyll Island meeting
The Aldrich Plan was adopted unchanged in 1913 and Glass-Owen was a separate piece of banking legislation passed in 1933 unrelated to the original Federal Reserve creation at all
context: Aldrich was Rockefeller's father-in-law. Paul Warburg (Kuhn Loeb) drafted much of the technical detail. Wilson signed the act two days before Christmas with most of Congress already departed.

question: Benjamin Strong was governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from 1914 until his death in 1928. Strong dominated Fed policy through informal channels with British central banker Montagu Norman, coordinating to keep US rates low so European countries could rebuild gold reserves after WWI. Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) blamed Strong for fueling the 1920s credit boom. What did Strong's coordination produce?
answer: Easy-money credit expansion in the late 1920s that inflated stocks and housing, setting up the boom that crashed in 1929 and the depression that followed for a decade
choices: Easy-money credit expansion in the late 1920s that inflated stocks and housing, setting up the boom that crashed in 1929 and the depression that followed for a decade
Tight-money discipline that kept the US economy growing steadily throughout the 1920s with no measurable contribution to the 1929 crash or any subsequent economic difficulties
Strong's policies had no measurable effect on US economic activity in the 1920s and the 1929 crash was caused entirely by speculation by individual investors without monetary causes
A balanced policy combining tight and easy money in alternating cycles that produced stable growth and was widely admired by Strong's successors throughout the rest of the 20th century
context: Strong's death in October 1928 left the Fed leaderless during the critical 1929-33 period. The internal Fed disputes (NY vs Washington, real-bills vs free-market) over how to respond to the crash contributed to the policy paralysis Friedman + Schwartz later blamed for the depression's depth.

question: Between 1929 and 1933, the US money supply (M1) fell by about one-third. Roughly 9,000 banks failed; depositors lost about $7 billion in savings. The Federal Reserve, with the legal authority to act as lender of last resort, did not. Friedman and Schwartz's 1963 A Monetary History argued this was the Fed's central failure. What policy choice produced the contraction?
answer: The Fed allowed bank failures to cascade by refusing to provide adequate emergency liquidity, on the 'real bills doctrine' view that liquidating bad banks was healthy
choices: The Fed allowed bank failures to cascade by refusing to provide adequate emergency liquidity, on the 'real bills doctrine' view that liquidating bad banks was healthy
The Fed aggressively expanded the money supply in 1929-33 but the contraction happened anyway due to private-sector deleveraging that the central bank could not influence
The Fed was legally prohibited from intervening before the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 and had no tools available to provide liquidity to failing banks during the entire period
The Fed actively printed money to cause the contraction as part of a deliberate political conspiracy to harm small banks and consolidate banking power among the large New York institutions
context: Bernanke's 2002 'I'd like to say to Milton and Anna: we did it, we're very sorry, but we won't do it again' speech (Friedman's 90th birthday) was the Fed's formal acknowledgment of the 1929-33 failure. Whether the post-2008 response actually avoided the mistake or repeated it in different form is contested.

question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published A Monetary History of the United States 1867-1960 in 1963 after about 15 years of research at NBER. The 860-page work changed how the Great Depression is taught. Their core thesis: the Depression was not an inevitable consequence of 1920s excesses, but a Fed policy failure. What is the broader recognition that follows from their argument?
answer: Central-bank decisions can turn ordinary recessions into depressions, so the institutional design of the Fed deserves as much scrutiny as the business cycles it claims to manage
choices: Central-bank decisions can turn ordinary recessions into depressions, so the institutional design of the Fed deserves as much scrutiny as the business cycles it claims to manage
Central-bank decisions have no measurable effect on aggregate economic activity, so the Friedman-Schwartz volume is interesting history but provides no policy lessons for any modern central bank
Central banks are necessary because Friedman-Schwartz proved no economy can function without one, and the volume is the canonical reference for modern central-bank-supremacy arguments
Friedman and Schwartz were Marxist economists whose volume argued for the abolition of capitalism, and their work has been used to justify centrally planned economies in postwar Europe and Asia
context: Anna Schwartz was the unsung hand on the research side; Friedman supplied the public-intellectual presence. The volume's documentary discipline (every claim sourced to Fed records, Treasury reports, contemporary newspapers) remains a model for the genre.

question: Paul Volcker, nominated by Carter in August 1979 and reappointed by Reagan in 1983, raised the federal funds rate to over 20% by June 1981 to break the entrenched inflation of the 1970s. Unemployment rose to 10.8% in 1982. Farmers drove tractors to the Fed building in Washington in protest. CPI inflation fell from 13.5% (1980) to 3.2% (1983). What did Volcker demonstrate?
answer: Persistent inflation can be broken by a central bank willing to cause politically painful recessions to restore monetary credibility, but only if the political will exists to absorb the cost
choices: Persistent inflation can be broken by a central bank willing to cause politically painful recessions to restore monetary credibility, but only if the political will exists to absorb the cost
Inflation always falls naturally without any central-bank action, and the 1980s decline in CPI was caused entirely by changes in OPEC oil pricing strategy with no monetary contribution
High interest rates have no effect on inflation, and the Volcker disinflation was actually a coincidence with the natural end of the 1970s inflationary spiral through other unrelated mechanisms
Volcker actually cut interest rates in 1981 and the inflation decline was caused by the rate cuts rather than by the much smaller earlier increases that were politically symbolic only
context: Volcker's willingness to break inflation at high political cost is the canonical counterexample to public-choice predictions that central bankers will always inflate. The discipline did not survive: post-Volcker Fed chairs have presided over expanding balance sheets and serial bailouts.

question: Beginning with the October 19, 1987 Black Monday crash, Alan Greenspan's Federal Reserve repeatedly cut rates to support falling asset markets: 1987 crash, 1998 LTCM/Russia, 2001 dot-com crash, 2003 jobless recovery. Markets came to expect a 'Greenspan put' — central-bank rate cuts cushioning every selloff. What economic distortion does this create?
answer: Moral hazard, in which investors take excessive risks knowing the Fed will socialize losses by cutting rates whenever asset markets decline, encouraging more risk-taking
choices: Moral hazard, in which investors take excessive risks knowing the Fed will socialize losses by cutting rates whenever asset markets decline, encouraging more risk-taking
No distortion, since the Fed's intervention restores normal market function and there is no measurable change in risk-taking behavior by investors as a result of expected rate cuts
A negative distortion, since investors actually reduce risk-taking when they expect Fed intervention, leading to under-investment in productive enterprises across the economy
The Greenspan put is a media fiction with no basis in actual Fed policy, and rate cuts during the 1987-2008 period were entirely uncorrelated with any movements in asset markets
context: The 'Bernanke put' and 'Yellen put' and 'Powell put' continued the pattern under successive Fed chairs. The 2008 GFC is often interpreted as the bill coming due on a generation of moral-hazard-encouraged risk-taking; the 2020 pandemic response massively expanded the underlying habit.

question: On March 14, 2008, the Federal Reserve provided emergency funding to JP Morgan Chase to acquire failing investment bank Bear Stearns for $2 per share (later raised to $10). The Fed guaranteed about $30 billion of Bear's distressed assets through a special-purpose vehicle (Maiden Lane). The action used Section 13(3) emergency powers not used since the 1930s. What precedent did this set?
answer: The Fed extended its lender-of-last-resort function from commercial banks to investment banks, signaling that 'too big to fail' applied to Wall Street firms outside its traditional regulatory perimeter
choices: The Fed extended its lender-of-last-resort function from commercial banks to investment banks, signaling that 'too big to fail' applied to Wall Street firms outside its traditional regulatory perimeter
The Fed declined to intervene with Bear Stearns and the firm was liquidated through ordinary bankruptcy proceedings with no use of emergency lending authority by any federal agency
The Fed nationalized Bear Stearns under direct federal ownership, and the firm continued to operate as a government-owned investment bank until being sold back to private investors in 2015
The Fed's intervention was authorized by Congress through a specific statute passed in March 2008 just before the Bear Stearns rescue, and was not based on any pre-existing emergency authority
context: The Lehman decision six months later (Sept 15, 2008 — let Lehman fail) puzzled the market: why was Bear saved and Lehman not? Bernanke's later explanation pointed to legal technicalities (collateral inadequacy) but the inconsistency rattled the system.

question: On Sunday September 14, 2008, Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson and Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke met with Wall Street CEOs at the NY Fed. They declined to backstop Lehman Brothers. Lehman filed for bankruptcy at 1:45am Monday September 15 — the largest bankruptcy in US history at $639 billion in assets. The next day AIG received an $85 billion Fed bridge loan. What did the contrast reveal?
answer: The selective bailout decisions were political and ad-hoc, not principled, so markets read the message that Fed-Treasury support depended on connections rather than legal rules
choices: The selective bailout decisions were political and ad-hoc, not principled, so markets read the message that Fed-Treasury support depended on connections rather than legal rules
The bailout decisions were strictly rule-based, with Lehman failing automatic legal criteria for federal support and AIG meeting them through a clearly defined collateral test
Lehman was not actually allowed to fail and the firm continued operations under federal ownership until 2012, with the 2008 bankruptcy filing being a media-manufactured event
AIG was allowed to fail and ordinary bankruptcy proceedings were used, with the $85 billion figure being a media exaggeration of routine Federal Reserve liquidity operations
context: Lehman CEO Dick Fuld's memoir and the FCIC report (Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission 2011) document the bailout decisions. AIG's bailout ultimately reached $182 billion. About $100 billion went through AIG to Goldman Sachs and other counterparties at 100 cents on the dollar — the so-called 'backdoor bailout'.

question: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of October 3, 2008 created TARP (Troubled Asset Relief Program), authorizing $700 billion in Treasury purchases of toxic assets and direct equity injections into banks. The vote initially failed in the House September 29 (Dow fell 778 points). It passed October 3 after sweeteners. What does TARP illustrate?
answer: When a financial crisis becomes acute enough, political resistance to bailouts collapses, so 'too big to fail' effectively negates democratic constraints once contagion is feared
choices: When a financial crisis becomes acute enough, political resistance to bailouts collapses, so 'too big to fail' effectively negates democratic constraints once contagion is feared
Democratic constraints on bailouts are highly effective and TARP was actually rejected by Congress, with the $700 billion being authorized through executive action only by the Treasury
TARP was a small program with no measurable effect on the financial system, and the actual recovery from the 2008 crisis was driven entirely by private-sector deleveraging without intervention
TARP was used exclusively to purchase toxic mortgage assets at market prices and the equity injections into banks happened through a separate program with full congressional approval at each stage
context: Direct equity injections into the nine largest US banks happened October 13-14, 2008 — Paulson convened the CEOs at Treasury and informed them they would accept federal capital. Net TARP losses to taxpayers were eventually small; the precedent established was large.

question: The Federal Reserve's balance sheet stood at about $870 billion in August 2007. By the end of QE3 (October 2014) it had reached about $4.5 trillion. QE1 (Nov 2008-Mar 2010): $1.25T mortgage-backed securities + $300B Treasuries. QE2 (Nov 2010-June 2011): $600B Treasuries. QE3 (Sep 2012-Oct 2014): $85B/month open-ended. What was the substantive theory underlying QE?
answer: Lower long-term rates and inflated asset prices would induce wealth-effect spending and investment, even though the prior 'zero lower bound' suggested traditional monetary policy was exhausted
choices: Lower long-term rates and inflated asset prices would induce wealth-effect spending and investment, even though the prior 'zero lower bound' suggested traditional monetary policy was exhausted
QE was designed to directly inject cash into household bank accounts to stimulate consumer spending, similar to a universal basic income program implemented through the central bank
QE was a routine open-market operation with no special theoretical justification and no measurable difference from ordinary Federal Reserve policy under chairmen Greenspan or Volcker in any era
QE was a fiscal program disguised as monetary policy, with the Federal Reserve directly purchasing goods and services from US households on behalf of the federal government for several years
context: The wealth-effect channel worked: asset prices recovered strongly, with the S&P 500 quadrupling from March 2009 to early 2020. The distributional consequences (Cantillon effect — gains concentrated among asset holders) are now widely acknowledged, including by Fed officials in retirement.

question: Between March and December 2020 the Federal Reserve expanded its balance sheet from $4T to over $7T, cut the funds rate to 0-0.25%, and launched corporate and municipal lending. Congress passed CARES ($2.2T) and additional packages through December. Total 2020-21 fiscal response approached $5T. What concerned sound-money critics?
answer: This scale of combined monetary and fiscal expansion in peacetime had no precedent and would either show up as inflation, as asset bubbles, or as both, with savers paying the bill
choices: This scale of combined monetary and fiscal expansion in peacetime had no precedent and would either show up as inflation, as asset bubbles, or as both, with savers paying the bill
The 2020 monetary and fiscal response was modest by historical standards and similar to ordinary recessionary policy used in many prior US recessions throughout the 20th century
Sound-money critics supported the 2020 response and there was no significant Austrian-school critique of the policies pursued by Powell, Mnuchin, and the congressional leadership during the year
The 2020 monetary expansion was funded entirely by foreign central banks rather than by Federal Reserve money creation, so it had no measurable effect on the US money supply during this period
context: Inflation appeared in 2021 and peaked at 9.1% CPI year-on-year in June 2022. Asset prices set records through 2021. The 2022 stock market correction and 2023 banking turmoil (SVB, Signature, First Republic, Credit Suisse) were the partial bill coming due. The longer-term consequences remain to be settled.

question: Stephanie Kelton's The Deficit Myth (2020) became the most popular statement of Modern Monetary Theory. Core thesis: a country issuing its own currency cannot 'run out of money' the way a household can; the only constraint on government spending is inflation, not solvency. The 2021-23 US inflation reached 9.1% (June 2022 peak). What did the real-world test reveal?
answer: When the inflation constraint MMT acknowledged arrived, it arrived larger, faster, and more persistent than the framework's popular deployment suggested, falsifying MMT's permissive policy implications
choices: When the inflation constraint MMT acknowledged arrived, it arrived larger, faster, and more persistent than the framework's popular deployment suggested, falsifying MMT's permissive policy implications
MMT was vindicated since inflation returned to 3% by 2023, demonstrating that the framework provides accurate guidance for fiscal-monetary policy under any post-pandemic conditions in any country
MMT made no predictions about inflation and the 2021-23 episode has no bearing on the theory, which is purely a description of accounting identities with no empirical content of any kind
MMT was abandoned by Kelton in 2022 and the framework no longer has any active proponents in academic or policy circles, having been definitively refuted by Larry Summers in his February 2021 op-ed
context: Kelton herself acknowledged the inflation constraint in her formal academic work. The political deployment of MMT systematically downplayed the constraint. The popular case for MMT aged poorly through 2021-23.

question: On February 4, 2021, former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers wrote a Washington Post op-ed warning that Biden's American Rescue Plan ($1.9T on top of December 2020's $900B) was several times larger than the output gap and would cause inflation. The piece was attacked as fear-mongering. Inflation hit 9.1% by June 2022. What does Summers's warning illustrate?
answer: Even a center-left economist applying basic macroeconomic arithmetic was vindicated by inflation that the policy consensus dismissed, revealing how ideologically captive the policy consensus had become
choices: Even a center-left economist applying basic macroeconomic arithmetic was vindicated by inflation that the policy consensus dismissed, revealing how ideologically captive the policy consensus had become
Summers's warning was attention-seeking and the 2021-23 inflation was caused entirely by supply-chain disruptions from COVID with no contribution from any fiscal or monetary expansion at any time

Summers retracted his warning in late 2021 after the Biden administration's fiscal advisers persuaded him the inflation forecast was wrong, with the 2022 inflation coming as a surprise to all economists
Summers's warning was correct only by chance and his methodology had no merit, since the inflation could equally have been zero given the underlying randomness of price-level dynamics in 2021
context: Summers had served as Clinton's Treasury Secretary and as a senior Obama economic adviser. His vindication is awkward for both the Biden-era center-left and the academic profession that lined up against him. The mainstream's failure to model the inflation correctly is the bigger story.

question: US CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% year-on-year in June 2022, the highest since November 1981. Producer prices peaked higher. The Fed had begun raising rates from 0 in March 2022; the fed funds rate reached 5.25-5.50% by July 2023. Inflation fell to ~3% by mid-2023. What was the central recognition for sound-money observers?
answer: Inflation is a monetary phenomenon when the cumulative excess money creation exceeds productive capacity growth, regardless of whether mainstream macro models predict it correctly in advance
choices: Inflation is a monetary phenomenon when the cumulative excess money creation exceeds productive capacity growth, regardless of whether mainstream macro models predict it correctly in advance
Inflation has no monetary cause and the 2021-23 episode was caused entirely by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 with no contribution from prior monetary or fiscal policy decisions
Inflation is always 2% or below in modern economies and the 2022 measurement was an aberration caused by statistical-reporting errors at the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the post-pandemic period
Inflation is irrelevant to monetary policy and the Federal Reserve's rate increases in 2022-23 were unnecessary, with the price level decline happening through unrelated supply-side factors only
context: Friedman's 1963 dictum 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' was widely mocked through the 2010s low-inflation era. The 2021-23 inflation made the dictum look prescient again. The mechanism (Cantillon effect, money supply transmission to asset and then consumer prices) operated roughly as Austrian theory predicts.

question: John Maynard Keynes's General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) was the most influential economics book of the 20th century. Its core claim: markets do not automatically clear at full employment, and government deficit spending can lift the economy out of slumps through the multiplier effect. What is the Austrian critique of the General Theory's foundational move?
answer: Keynes treated capital as a homogeneous aggregate, ignoring the structure of production (stages, durations, interest-rate sensitivity) that determines whether stimulus produces real growth or merely malinvestment
choices: Keynes treated capital as a homogeneous aggregate, ignoring the structure of production (stages, durations, interest-rate sensitivity) that determines whether stimulus produces real growth or merely malinvestment
Austrian economists agreed with the General Theory and Hayek wrote a positive review in 1936 praising Keynes's analytical framework, with the Austrian-Keynesian divide being a postwar invention
The General Theory was rejected by every contemporary economist of note in 1936 and was only rediscovered in the 1970s after a long period of complete obscurity
The General Theory is a Marxist work and the Austrian critique focused on its rejection of capitalism rather than on any specific analytical claims about employment, interest, or money
context: Hayek's 1931 review of Keynes's Treatise on Money was the canonical Austrian critique of the pre-General-Theory Keynes. Hayek's failure to write a comparable response to the General Theory itself is one of the historical 'what ifs' of 20th-century economics. Rothbard, Garrison, and Hülsmann developed the response posthumously.

question: Keynes's General Theory introduces 'animal spirits', the irrational psychological currents that drive entrepreneurial investment beyond rational calculation. Akerlof and Shiller revived it in their 2009 Animal Spirits. What is the Austrian objection to animal spirits as a stand-alone explanation of investment cycles?
answer: Investment cycles correlate systematically with monetary policy and credit expansion; 'animal spirits' is an unfalsifiable label that conceals rather than explains the boom-bust pattern Mises and Hayek named
choices: Investment cycles correlate systematically with monetary policy and credit expansion; 'animal spirits' is an unfalsifiable label that conceals rather than explains the boom-bust pattern Mises and Hayek named

Austrians accept the animal-spirits explanation fully and the entire Austrian Business Cycle Theory is identical to Keynes's framework with different terminology applied to the same underlying psychological dynamics

Animal spirits is the central Austrian concept and was originated by Menger in 1871, with Keynes borrowing the idea without attribution in his 1936 General Theory under a slightly modified terminology

Investment cycles do not actually exist and the apparent boom-bust pattern is a statistical illusion, so the question of animal spirits versus monetary explanation has no factual content for any economist
context: The Austrian objection is that 'animal spirits' is non-falsifiable: any investment decline can be attributed to psychological retreat after the fact, with no predictive content. ABCT, by contrast, predicts investment patterns based on monetary expansion below the natural interest rate. The 2008 GFC was a clean test, and Austrians won it.

question: The Phillips curve, charted by A.W. Phillips in 1958, showed an inverse relationship between UK unemployment and wage growth. Samuelson and Solow translated it for US policy. The 1960s consensus held policymakers could choose a point: higher inflation for lower unemployment. The 1970s stagflation broke it. What did Friedman's 1968 lecture predict?
answer: Workers and firms would build inflation expectations into wage and price decisions, shifting the curve up, so there is no stable trade-off, only a temporary one that erodes over time
choices: Workers and firms would build inflation expectations into wage and price decisions, shifting the curve up, so there is no stable trade-off, only a temporary one that erodes over time

The Phillips curve is a stable empirical regularity that has held throughout the 20th century with no breakdown, and the 1970s stagflation was a statistical artifact rather than a real economic phenomenon
The Phillips curve was vindicated by the 1970s data, with the apparent stagflation being a misreading of the relationship between wage growth and unemployment rather than a genuine model failure
Friedman supported the Phillips curve and his 1968 lecture endorsed its use for monetary policy, with the curve only being criticized by Friedman much later in his 1980s public writings on the topic
context: Friedman's 'The Role of Monetary Policy' (American Economic Review 1968, presidential address) predicted the breakdown before it happened. Edmund Phelps reached similar conclusions independently. The expectations-augmented Phillips curve became the mainstream model after the 1970s; the deeper lesson — that stable monetary trade-offs are illusory — is still resisted.

question: Hayek's Prices and Production (1931) is the canonical statement of the Austrian Business Cycle Theory. Hayek diagrammed the economy as stages of production, from raw materials through intermediate goods to consumer goods, each requiring time. Lowering interest rates artificially lengthens the production structure beyond what real savings support, producing malinvestment. When the boom corrects, what happens?
answer: Capital tied up in unprofitable longer-stage projects must be liquidated, workers must move between sectors, and the recession is the needed correction of the prior monetary distortion
choices: Capital tied up in unprofitable longer-stage projects must be liquidated, workers must move between sectors, and the recession is the needed correction of the prior monetary distortion
Capital adjusts smoothly with no recession, since markets price information immediately and there are no real economic costs from monetary policy shifts under any circumstances at all
The central bank prevents the recession through countercyclical policy and there is no period of correction, with the boom merely transitioning into a permanent higher-growth steady state
Workers cannot move between sectors so the recession affects only specific industries, with aggregate output and employment unaffected by the monetary distortion or its eventual correction
context: Hayek's Hayekian triangles diagram the production structure visually. The 1931 lectures at LSE were the moment Austrian theory entered the English-speaking academy. Hayek's 1974 Nobel cited his cycle theory specifically. The 2008 GFC's pattern (housing-construction boom from Fed easy money, then capital liquidation) matches the Hayek framework cleanly.

question: Ludwig von Mises's The Theory of Money and Credit (1912) was the first systematic Austrian treatment of money. Mises extended Carl Menger's 1871 marginal-utility framework to money, solving what came to be called the 'Mises regression theorem': money's value can be traced back through time to its original commodity-money use. What problem does the regression theorem solve?
answer: Why people accept money today (its prior purchasing power gives current expectations) ultimately grounding money's value in past commodity use rather than circular subjective valuation
choices: Why people accept money today (its prior purchasing power gives current expectations) ultimately grounding money's value in past commodity use rather than circular subjective valuation
Why money is necessary for economic activity at all, since the regression theorem proves that barter economies are impossible due to the double-coincidence-of-wants problem unsolvable otherwise
Why central banks should issue currency rather than private banks, since the regression theorem requires governmental backing to establish initial commodity-money status for any monetary unit
Why fiat money cannot exist according to Mises, since the regression theorem mathematically proves that all sustainable monetary systems must remain fully convertible to a specific physical commodity
context: The regression theorem became controversial again with Bitcoin. Critics argued Bitcoin cannot be money because it has no prior commodity use; defenders argued Bitcoin's monetary properties (scarcity, divisibility, fungibility, durability, recognizability, portability) bootstrap its monetary status without need for a commodity origin. The debate is unresolved among Austrians.

question: In 1931 Hayek wrote a critical review of Keynes's Treatise on Money in Economica. Keynes responded by reviewing Hayek's Prices and Production. Both grew frustrated with the other's failure to engage. Hayek did not write a comparable response to Keynes's General Theory (1936). Why is this absence a major regret?
answer: The General Theory dominated postwar policy without facing the sustained Austrian critique Hayek had given the Treatise, so Keynesianism became consensus partly by default rather than by winning the argument
choices: The General Theory dominated postwar policy without facing the sustained Austrian critique Hayek had given the Treatise, so Keynesianism became consensus partly by default rather than by winning the argument

Hayek's 1936 review of the General Theory was the canonical Austrian response and was widely cited in subsequent economic literature, making the postwar Keynesian dominance entirely a matter of argument
The Treatise on Money was actually more influential than the General Theory and Hayek's critique of the Treatise effectively defeated Keynes's framework in the academic mainstream during the 1930s
Hayek and Keynes were close personal friends and never engaged in any public economic debate, with the 'Hayek-Keynes debate' being a postwar invention by Rothbard and his followers in the 1970s
context: Hayek later said he had hesitated to respond because Keynes's framework kept shifting. He also worked on his political-philosophy book The Road to Serfdom (1944) during the war years. The Mont Pelerin Society he founded in 1947 became the institutional vehicle for the classical-liberal counter-tradition.

question: Obama's $787B American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (Feb 2009) was sold on a fiscal multiplier of ~1.5: every $1 spent would produce $1.50 of GDP. The Romer-Romer projections forecast unemployment peaking under 8% with stimulus, above 9% without. Actual unemployment peaked at 10% in October 2009 with the stimulus in effect. Why did unemployment peak ABOVE the no-stimulus forecast?
answer: The fiscal multiplier was smaller than Keynesian models predicted — likely below 1.0 — so spending crowded out private activity rather than adding to it on net
choices: The fiscal multiplier was smaller than Keynesian models predicted — likely below 1.0 — so spending crowded out private activity rather than adding to it on net
The multiplier was higher than predicted at over 3.0 — the actual outcome vastly exceeded Romer-Romer projections, vindicating Keynesian fiscal theory
The multiplier was exactly 1.5 as predicted — the 10% peak was attributable to mid-2009 demographic factors only and not policy effectiveness
The multiplier was negative — the ARRA actively caused the unemployment increase, a finding endorsed by mainstream Keynesian economics consensus
context: The Romer-Romer projections were public in early 2009. The actual outcome was substantially worse. The episode is often cited (Cochrane, Cogan, Taylor, Wieland) as evidence that headline-Keynesian multipliers overstate fiscal stimulus efficacy. The 2020-21 stimulus produced inflation rather than the expected real-output expansion.

question: Central-bank independence became a fashionable institutional-design principle in the 1980s-90s. The argument: politicians have short horizons and pressure central banks to inflate before elections, so insulating monetary policy from democratic accountability protects long-run price stability. Bundesbank, RBNZ (1989), BoE (1997) became models. What does the capture critique add?
answer: Independence from elected officials still leaves central banks captured by the financial sector they regulate, swapping political accountability for industry capture rather than eliminating it
choices: Independence from elected officials still leaves central banks captured by the financial sector they regulate, swapping political accountability for industry capture rather than eliminating it
Central-bank independence has fully solved the problem of monetary capture and there are no remaining concerns about whose interests independent central banks actually serve in any practice
Central banks are not independent in practice and are still directly controlled by elected officials, making the 1980s-90s institutional reforms cosmetic changes with no measurable effects at all
Industry capture of central banks has no measurable effect on monetary policy and the concept of regulatory capture does not apply to central banking under any reasonable definitional analysis
context: Stigler 1971 'Theory of Economic Regulation' is the foundational text. The Fed-Treasury-Wall Street revolving door (Rubin, Paulson, Geithner, Yellen) is the canonical example. Independence from voters is not the same as independence from concentrated economic interests.

question: The Fed-Treasury-Wall Street revolving door is structural to US financial policymaking. Robert Rubin: Goldman Sachs to Treasury Secretary to Citigroup (where he received ~$115M while Citigroup needed bailouts). Hank Paulson: Goldman CEO to Treasury Secretary in the 2008 crisis. Janet Yellen: Fed Chair to Treasury Secretary. What concern does this raise?
answer: The same people who set policy go on to high-paying positions at firms benefiting from those policies, distorting incentives toward favorable treatment for future employers
choices: The same people who set policy go on to high-paying positions at firms benefiting from those policies, distorting incentives toward favorable treatment for future employers
The revolving door has no measurable effect on policy decisions and the same officials would make identical choices if their post-government careers were restricted by binding contractual rules
The revolving door is a media fiction and former Treasury Secretaries rarely take private-sector positions after government service, instead retiring to academic or charitable roles afterward
The revolving door flows in one direction only, with private-sector executives entering government but never leaving for private positions, so concerns about bias are unfounded as a result
context: The pattern is bipartisan. Geithner: Treasury to NY Fed President to Treasury Secretary to Warburg Pincus president. The Rubin-Paulson-Geithner-Yellen sequence concentrated bailout-determination power in a small social network. Public choice predicts and explains the pattern.

question: Greece joined the euro in 2001. The 2010 sovereign-debt crisis exposed long-running fiscal deficits hidden by Goldman Sachs currency-swap accounting. Greek bond yields spiked to 30%+ in 2012. The 'troika' (ECB, European Commission, IMF) imposed austerity for bailouts totaling ~286 billion euros. The 2015 Tsipras referendum rejected the conditions but Syriza accepted them anyway. What did the crisis reveal?
answer: A currency union without a fiscal union is structurally unstable; countries cannot devalue out of crises and are locked into politically explosive internal-deflation adjustments
choices: A currency union without a fiscal union is structurally unstable; countries cannot devalue out of crises and are locked into politically explosive internal-deflation adjustments
The eurozone is perfectly stable and the Greek crisis was caused by Greek fiscal misbehavior with no structural eurozone design flaws contributing to the persistence of the recession
The eurozone was secretly dissolved in 2015 and replaced with a new currency arrangement, with the Greek crisis being the publicly visible portion of a larger institutional restructuring
Greece left the eurozone in 2015 after the referendum and adopted a new drachma, with the eurozone continuing to function without Greek membership from that point onward in monetary history
context: Robert Mundell's 'optimum currency area' theory (1961) anticipated the eurozone's structural problem decades before. The political failure to act on the theory's implications is the deeper story. The euro survived; the contradiction did not resolve. Italy, Spain, and France carry the risk forward.

question: On July 26, 2012, ECB President Mario Draghi told a London conference: 'Within our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.' Italian and Spanish bond yields fell sharply over following weeks. Draghi never had to deploy the OMT (Outright Monetary Transactions) program in size. What did the speech reveal?
answer: A credible threat of unlimited intervention can move markets without requiring intervention, but only when the central bank has both legal authority and political backing to follow through
choices: A credible threat of unlimited intervention can move markets without requiring intervention, but only when the central bank has both legal authority and political backing to follow through
Central-bank verbal interventions have no measurable effect on markets and the Italian and Spanish bond yield declines after July 2012 were caused entirely by unrelated supply-and-demand factors
Draghi was forced to deploy massive bond purchases immediately after the speech and the 'whatever it takes' line was a coincidence rather than a market-moving event in eurozone history that year
The ECB had no authority to make the statement and Draghi was personally censured by the European Council for exceeding his mandate, with the speech being formally repudiated within only weeks
context: The German Constitutional Court eventually challenged the OMT framework but never invalidated it. The 'whatever it takes' speech is studied as a canonical case of rhetorical central-banking. The deeper question (whether the underlying contradictions are merely deferred) remains open through Lagarde.

question: Fed Chair Jerome Powell spent most of 2021 calling the post-COVID inflation 'transitory'. By November 30, 2021, he retired the word. The Fed began raising rates in March 2022 (25bps), then 50bps in May, then four 75bps hikes through November. The funds rate reached 4.25-4.50% by year-end, from 0 in March. What does the 2021-22 sequence illustrate?
answer: Central banks systematically underestimate inflation when political-economic incentives favor accommodation, and only act decisively once the political cost of inaction exceeds the cost of recession
choices: Central banks systematically underestimate inflation when political-economic incentives favor accommodation, and only act decisively once the political cost of inaction exceeds the cost of recession
Central banks are accurate forecasters of inflation and the 2021 'transitory' framing was correct since inflation did eventually return to target levels by the end of the disinflation cycle in 2023
Central banks have no incentive to underestimate inflation and Powell's 2021 statements reflected the best available macro models without any political or institutional bias toward accommodation
Central banks always act preemptively against inflation and the 2021-22 sequence was an exception caused by unusual COVID-era data noise that misled an otherwise highly responsive monetary framework
context: The 'transitory' framing aged poorly. Summers's February 2021 warning and other Austrian and monetarist warnings preceded the Fed's recognition by about a year. The delay shows up in the 9.1% peak inflation and the savings of fixed-income households eroded during that period.

question: From December 2008 through December 2015 the Fed held the federal funds rate at 0-0.25% (Zero Interest Rate Policy, ZIRP). Real rates were negative for much of the period. Asset prices rose strongly. Saving in bank deposits earned negative real returns. What is the Austrian recognition about a sustained near-zero rate regime?
answer: Persistent below-natural rates distort capital allocation, encourage debt accumulation, inflate asset prices, and tax savers who provide the real capital the economy needs for productive investment
choices: Persistent below-natural rates distort capital allocation, encourage debt accumulation, inflate asset prices, and tax savers who provide the real capital the economy needs for productive investment
Persistent near-zero rates have no distributional consequences and produce identical outcomes for savers and asset holders, with the wealth gap remaining unchanged through any monetary policy regime
Persistent near-zero rates eliminate the business cycle by smoothing investment over time and are recommended as permanent policy by Austrian economists for that reason in their academic writings

The 2008-15 ZIRP period had no measurable effect on US asset prices and the strong equity-market rally during this time was driven entirely by improved corporate fundamentals unrelated to monetary policy
context: The ZIRP era's distributional consequences (asset-holders won, savers and renters lost) became a major political issue in the 2016 election. The Fed's policy frame focused on aggregate employment without giving distributional weight to the Cantillon-effect transfer the policy enacted.

question: The ECB under Mario Draghi introduced negative interest rates on bank reserves in June 2014. The Bank of Japan went negative in January 2016. By 2019 about $17T in global sovereign debt traded at negative yields, with investors paying governments to hold money. The policies aimed to force banks to lend rather than hoard reserves. What did the NIRP era reveal?
answer: Below-zero rates produced limited extra lending and substantial financial-sector distortion (margin compression, asset bubbles, currency competition) without delivering promised growth
choices: Below-zero rates produced limited extra lending and substantial financial-sector distortion (margin compression, asset bubbles, currency competition) without delivering promised growth
Negative interest rates have been an unqualified success in stimulating economic growth and are now permanent policy in the eurozone and Japan with widespread support from economists today
Negative interest rates had no measurable effect on financial markets or lending behavior and were essentially cosmetic policies adopted by central banks for political-signaling purposes for years
Negative interest rates caused immediate hyperinflation in the eurozone and Japan, which is why both central banks abandoned the policy within months of introduction without any sustained NIRP period
context: The NIRP era prompted a wave of 'why hold cash in a bank' analyses and indirectly contributed to Bitcoin's institutional adoption. The Swiss National Bank's deeper negative rates (-0.75% peak) were a particularly stark case. NIRP was abandoned across most jurisdictions in the 2022-23 hiking cycle.

question: The BoJ pioneered modern unconventional monetary policy beginning the early 2000s. QE ran 2001-2006, then relaunched as 'Quantitative and Qualitative Easing' (QQE) under Governor Kuroda from April 2013 with a 2% inflation target. The BoJ became Japan's largest holder of government bonds and a major equity-ETF holder. Inflation hit 2% only briefly. What did Japan teach?
answer: Open-ended QE can suppress yields and elevate asset prices for years without sustained inflation in a high-savings society, at the cost of central-bank balance-sheet dominance over markets
choices: Open-ended QE can suppress yields and elevate asset prices for years without sustained inflation in a high-savings society, at the cost of central-bank balance-sheet dominance over markets

QE always produces immediate hyperinflation regardless of underlying economic conditions, and the Japanese experience contradicted basic monetary theory in ways that have never been adequately explained
QE has no measurable effect on any economic variable and the Japanese experiments with unconventional policy 2001-2024 had no consequences for Japanese asset prices or for the yen exchange rate
The BoJ abandoned QE in 2010 after concluding it had no effect on inflation, and Japanese monetary policy returned to conventional interest-rate management for the entire post-2010 period since
context: The BoJ's experience anticipated much of the post-2008 Fed and ECB toolkit. The 'Japanification' thesis (slow growth, falling labor force, deflation, central-bank dominance) was applied to Europe and floated for the US. The 2024 BoJ rate normalization is the first serious test of unwinding the regime.

question: A 'Credit Default Swap' (CDS) is insurance against a bond defaulting — buyer pays premiums; seller pays out if the bond fails. AIG was the world's largest insurer in 2008; its Financial Products division had sold ~$440B in CDS on mortgage securities with NO reserves. As mortgages crashed, AIG faced overwhelming margin calls. The Fed extended an $85B emergency loan Sept 16, 2008. Why did AIG's CDS exposure threaten the entire system?
answer: Every major bank had bought AIG-issued CDS protection — if AIG defaulted, banks worldwide would face simultaneous insurance failures; total federal commitments topped $182B
choices: Every major bank had bought AIG-issued CDS protection — if AIG defaulted, banks worldwide would face simultaneous insurance failures; total federal commitments topped $182B
AIG was the only US insurance company in 2008 — its failure would have eliminated all property and life insurance across the country for many years afterward
AIG held deeds to most American homes — its failure would have triggered automatic foreclosure on roughly 60% of US residential mortgages held by working families
AIG owned controlling stakes in every major bank — its failure would have liquidated the largest US banks via cross-shareholding, requiring federal takeover
context: AIG sold CDS without reserves because the senior tranches of mortgage securities were rated AAA — assumed never to fail. When housing collapsed, the 'impossible' losses hit. Goldman Sachs received $13B via AIG. The canonical 2008 moral-hazard moment.

question: The FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) sets US monetary policy. It has 12 voting members: 7 from the Board of Governors (presidential appointees, Senate-confirmed) and 5 from the 12 regional Fed Banks (NY Fed permanent; 4 rotate). The regional banks are technically private corporations owned by member commercial banks. What does this structure mean institutionally?
answer: Monetary policy is set by a body partly composed of representatives from privately owned regional banks owned by commercial banks, blending public and private authority in ways unique to federal agencies
choices: Monetary policy is set by a body partly composed of representatives from privately owned regional banks owned by commercial banks, blending public and private authority in ways unique to federal agencies
The Federal Reserve is a fully public agency with no private-bank participation in its policy decisions, and the 12 regional Fed Banks are simply subsidiary offices of the federal government itself
The Federal Reserve is a fully private corporation with no government oversight at all, and the Board of Governors is appointed by member banks rather than by the President of the United States
The FOMC has no authority to set US monetary policy, which is determined by the US Treasury, with the FOMC providing only ceremonial advisory opinions during their regular meetings
context: The hybrid structure is intentional: Aldrich Plan to Glass-Owen kept the regional-bank private-corporate framing for political reasons. Member commercial banks elect 6 of the 9 directors at each regional Reserve Bank. The 'public agency wearing private clothes' nature is why public choice applies.

question: The Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977 amended the Federal Reserve Act to give the Fed a 'dual mandate': maximum employment AND price stability. (A 'moderate long-term interest rates' goal is nominally included.) Before 1977, the Fed had no explicit congressional mandate. Why does the dual mandate create internal tension other central banks (Bundesbank, RBNZ, BoE) avoid?
answer: Price stability and full employment can conflict short-run, so the Fed must trade them off without explicit congressional guidance, leaving room for political pressure and discretion
choices: Price stability and full employment can conflict short-run, so the Fed must trade them off without explicit congressional guidance, leaving room for political pressure and discretion
Price stability and full employment never conflict and the dual mandate creates no policy tensions, with the Fed always able to pursue both goals simultaneously without any institutional difficulty
Other central banks have identical dual mandates and the Fed's institutional position is no different from the Bundesbank, RBNZ, or post-1997 Bank of England in any meaningful structural dimension
The 1977 Reform Act has been repealed and the Fed no longer has any explicit congressional mandate, returning to its pre-1977 status of being free to set its own goals without statutory direction
context: Bundesbank (pre-euro), RBNZ (1989), and BoE (1997) all moved to single-mandate (price stability) designs explicitly to escape the dual-mandate tension. The US dual mandate is consistently invoked to defend looser policy in slowdowns. The 2021-22 inflation surge restarted the long-running debate.

question: Mortgage securitization (Fannie Mae 1968 reform, Freddie Mac 1970) transformed home loans from bank-held assets into tradable bonds. By the mid-2000s, private-label MBS (mortgage-backed securities) packaged subprime loans, sold to global investors as AAA-rated. Credit rating agencies (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) collected fees from issuers. What was the structural problem?
answer: Originators no longer held the loans they made, so credit standards collapsed; rating agencies were paid by issuers, so AAA ratings were systematically inflated for fee income
choices: Originators no longer held the loans they made, so credit standards collapsed; rating agencies were paid by issuers, so AAA ratings were systematically inflated for fee income

Mortgage securitization improved credit standards by spreading risk and the 2008 crisis was caused entirely by unrelated factors with no contribution from the securitization process or rating agencies
Mortgage securitization was banned by the SEC in 2002 and the 2008 crisis involved no MBS issuance, with the entire collapse being caused by ordinary bank lending without any market-based instruments
Mortgage securitization was managed entirely by the federal government with no private-sector involvement, and the 2008 crisis was a pure governmental policy failure with no role for private actors
context: Michael Lewis's The Big Short (2010) and the FCIC Report (2011) document the structural-incentive failures. The Cassandras (Michael Burry, Greg Lippmann, Steve Eisman) saw it coming; the institutional mainstream did not. Friedrich Hayek's epistemic-failure framework explains the pattern.

question: Charles Ponzi's 1920 Boston scheme paid early investors with new investors' money — Bernie Madoff ran the same play for at least 17 years. Arrested Dec 11, 2008 after his sons reported him to the FBI. Defrauded ~$65B notional (~$19B real losses). Harry Markopolos warned the SEC since 2000; the SEC investigated five times and found nothing. Madoff got 150 years. Why was the mathematical proof ignored for nine years?
answer: SEC staff lacked both the technical math skill to follow the proof AND the institutional incentive to challenge a well-connected NASDAQ insider
choices: SEC staff lacked both the technical math skill to follow the proof AND the institutional incentive to challenge a well-connected NASDAQ insider
Markopolos was wrong, SEC investigations correctly found no fraud, and the 2008 collapse was caused by unrelated market conditions during the crisis
The SEC shut down Madoff back in 2002, and the 2008 arrest was an entirely separate matter unrelated to the earlier Ponzi-scheme allegations against him
Madoff wasn't actually running a Ponzi, the arrest was based on accounting errors since reversed, and the $65B figure was simply a media exaggeration
context: Charles Ponzi promised Boston investors 50% in 45 days in 1920 from postal-coupon arbitrage; his scheme collapsed in months and named the entire category. Markopolos's No One Would Listen (2010) details the SEC failure. Madoff was the former NASDAQ chairman with deep social ties to SEC officials. Regulatory capture compounded by competence gaps.

question: Glass-Steagall (Banking Act of 1933) separated commercial banking (deposit-taking, lending) from investment banking (underwriting, trading), in response to Depression-era bank failures. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 repealed key sections, allowing financial holding companies to combine activities. Citigroup formed from Travelers + Citibank ahead of repeal. What is the argument linking repeal to 2008?
answer: Combination let large banks use insured deposits to fund speculative trading, spread losses across the system, and made firms large enough to require bailouts when they failed
choices: Combination let large banks use insured deposits to fund speculative trading, spread losses across the system, and made firms large enough to require bailouts when they failed
Glass-Steagall repeal had no measurable effect on the 2008 crisis and was unrelated to any aspect of the system collapse, with the crisis being caused entirely by housing prices alone
Glass-Steagall was strengthened in 1999 rather than repealed, and the system in 2008 was substantially more separated than it had been in 1933 under FDR's New Deal program
Glass-Steagall repeal was rolled back in 2005 and was not in effect during the 2008 crisis, with the underlying institutional framework being identical to the pre-repeal 1933 structure
context: Clinton signed Gramm-Leach-Bliley with Treasury Secretary Larry Summers's support. Robert Rubin later joined Citigroup, becoming the canonical example of the revolving door. Post-2008 Dodd-Frank did not restore Glass-Steagall's separation.

question: The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (July 21, 2010) was the largest financial-regulatory overhaul since the New Deal. It created the CFPB, FSOC, Volcker Rule, and imposed enhanced capital requirements. By 2024 the largest US banks were larger than in 2008. What does Dodd-Frank illustrate?
answer: Complex regulatory frameworks tend to entrench the largest incumbents who can afford compliance costs, creating barriers to entry that consolidate the industry the regulation was supposed to discipline
choices: Complex regulatory frameworks tend to entrench the largest incumbents who can afford compliance costs, creating barriers to entry that consolidate the industry the regulation was supposed to discipline

Dodd-Frank successfully broke up the largest banks and the post-2010 financial system has many more small institutions than the pre-crisis system did, restoring competitive banking conditions in the US
Dodd-Frank has been entirely repealed and the post-2008 financial-regulatory framework is identical to the pre-2008 framework, with no Dodd-Frank-era requirements remaining in effect anywhere today
Dodd-Frank had no measurable effect on bank concentration and the 2010-2024 increase in large-bank market share was caused entirely by unrelated demographic and technology factors with no role
context: Public-choice theory predicted this outcome: incumbent firms shape regulation in their favor, and 'reform' often increases industry concentration rather than disciplining it. The Stigler 1971 capture framework explains the pattern. The 2023 SVB-Signature episode showed mid-tier banks remain vulnerable.

question: Silicon Valley Bank failed on March 10, 2023, the second-largest US bank failure ever. SVB held ~$200B in assets; ~95% of deposits were above the FDIC $250K insurance cap. SVB had loaded up on long-duration Treasuries during 2020-21, then took mark-to-market losses as Fed rate hikes pushed bond prices down. The run completed in 24 hours via Twitter and digital banking. What did regulators do?
answer: Treasury, Fed, FDIC invoked a 'systemic risk exception' to backstop ALL deposits (including uninsured), setting a precedent that raises the FDIC cap to infinity for large banks
choices: Treasury, Fed, FDIC invoked a 'systemic risk exception' to backstop ALL deposits (including uninsured), setting a precedent that raises the FDIC cap to infinity for large banks
Regulators applied standard FDIC rules and depositors with balances above $250K lost the uninsured portion of deposits, consistent with the pre-2023 framework for bank failures in the US
Regulators allowed SVB to recover without intervention and the bank continued operating normally after March 2023, with no federal action being required to stabilize the institution
Regulators nationalized SVB and the federal government continues to own the bank as of 2024, with no private-sector resolution of the March 2023 failure having taken place to date
context: Signature failed the same weekend; First Republic in early May; all received the systemic-risk treatment. Credit Suisse failed days later (UBS shotgun marriage backed by Swiss central bank). 'Too big to fail' expanded to 'too large to lose deposits' regardless of size or politics.

question: The 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks are technically owned by their member commercial banks, which must subscribe to stock equal to 6% of their capital and surplus. Members receive a 6% statutory dividend on paid-in stock. Member-bank shareholders elect 6 of the 9 directors of their regional Reserve Bank. Why does this matter for public-choice analysis?
answer: Direct ownership and director-election rights give member banks formal channels of influence on monetary policy the public lacks, embedding industry capture in the institution's legal structure
choices: Direct ownership and director-election rights give member banks formal channels of influence on monetary policy the public lacks, embedding industry capture in the institution's legal structure
Member-bank ownership is purely ceremonial and member banks have no influence over Fed policy through any formal or informal channels in the modern Federal Reserve System operating today
Member banks do not own Fed regional banks and the FOMC is composed entirely of presidential appointees with no industry representation, making the institution structurally insulated from capture
Member banks are owned by the Federal Reserve rather than the reverse, with regional Fed Banks holding equity stakes in member commercial banks rather than the other way around structurally
context: The structure dates to 1913 Glass-Owen as a political compromise: bankers wanted private control, populists wanted federal control, the hybrid satisfied neither but endured. The 6% dividend is paid out of Fed earnings before any remittance to the US Treasury.

question: Irving Fisher (1867-1947), the Yale monetary economist, proposed in 100% Money (1935) that commercial banks be required to hold 100% reserves against checking deposits. Credit creation would be separated from deposit-taking. Frank Knight, Henry Simons, and other Chicago economists endorsed the plan. The Chicago Plan was floated in 1933 and rejected. What does the proposal target?
answer: Fractional-reserve banking's instability: banks create deposit money via loans, expanding the money supply pro-cyclically and amplifying boom-bust cycles the central bank then tries to manage
choices: Fractional-reserve banking's instability: banks create deposit money via loans, expanding the money supply pro-cyclically and amplifying boom-bust cycles the central bank then tries to manage
The 100% reserve plan was not about banking and was instead a proposal for reforming the gold standard with no relation to fractional-reserve deposit creation or monetary-amplification effects
The Chicago Plan was adopted in 1933 and US banks have operated under 100% reserve requirements ever since, making fractional-reserve banking illegal in the US from the New Deal onward

Fisher's plan was a Marxist proposal for nationalizing all banks and the Chicago economists endorsing it were sympathizers of central planning, making the entire idea opposed to free-market principles
context: Murray Rothbard endorsed 100% reserves (with gold rather than paper) as the Austrian sound-money ideal. Mises and Hayek were more divided. Modern proposals (Kotlikoff's 'Limited Purpose Banking', Turner's narrow banking) revisit Fisher's framework. 2008 GFC reawakened the debate.

question: Bretton Woods (July 1944) created the IMF and the IBRD (later the World Bank). The IMF would lend to countries running balance-of-payments difficulties; the World Bank would fund postwar reconstruction and later development. Both bodies were headquartered in Washington under US influence. What does the architecture reveal?
answer: The postwar monetary system was designed as much for US geopolitical leadership as for monetary stability; the institutions' DC location and dollar-centricity embed US power in the global framework
choices: The postwar monetary system was designed as much for US geopolitical leadership as for monetary stability; the institutions' DC location and dollar-centricity embed US power in the global framework
The IMF and World Bank were designed as neutral technocratic institutions with no special relationship to US geopolitical interests and have been independent of US influence ever since 1944
The Bretton Woods institutions were never actually created and the postwar monetary system functioned without any formal international bodies until the 1971 Nixon shock dissolved the arrangement
The IMF and World Bank were headquartered in Geneva rather than Washington, and the postwar monetary system was designed to give equal influence to all 44 founding nations regardless of size
context: The IMF managing director is by tradition European; the World Bank president is by tradition American. The institutions' 'structural adjustment' lending (Africa, Latin America, post-Soviet states) became deeply controversial in the 1990s-2000s. Austrian economists are largely critical.

question: The Marshall Plan (1948-1951) provided ~$13.3B (~$170B in 2024 dollars) in US aid for Western European reconstruction. The program is credited with rapid postwar recovery in West Germany, France, Italy. The German Wirtschaftswunder, often attributed to the Plan, owed more to Ludwig Erhard's 1948 currency reform and free-market liberalization. Why does the distinction matter?
answer: Foreign aid can support recovery only when domestic policies (property rights, sound money, free markets) make productive use of resources; aid without reform produces dependency
choices: Foreign aid can support recovery only when domestic policies (property rights, sound money, free markets) make productive use of resources; aid without reform produces dependency
Foreign aid is sufficient on its own to produce economic recovery regardless of domestic policies, and the Marshall Plan demonstrated this principle which has been confirmed in every subsequent case
The Marshall Plan was actually a failure and West German recovery happened despite the program rather than because of it, with the postwar economic miracle being explained by other factors entirely
The Marshall Plan was the only factor in West German recovery and Erhard's 1948 currency reform had no measurable effect on the economic outcome of the postwar period in Germany or elsewhere
context: Ludwig Erhard, Hayek-influenced and Austrian-aligned, abolished price controls and replaced the Reichsmark with the Deutsche mark in June 1948 against Allied skepticism. Eastern Europe's postwar trajectory is the counterfactual: same aid offered Stalin refused, opposite institutional choices.

question: On June 20, 1948, Ludwig Erhard, economics director of the British-American Bizone, abolished postwar price controls and replaced the worthless Reichsmark with the new Deutsche mark at 10:1. Allied authorities had not approved the price-control liberalization; Erhard acted on his own. Within days, shop windows filled with hoarded goods. Black markets collapsed. What changed inside one day?
answer: Markets respond rapidly to sound money and free prices; the German postwar miracle began with a 24-hour shock that ended scarcity by ending the price controls and currency debasement causing it
choices: Markets respond rapidly to sound money and free prices; the German postwar miracle began with a 24-hour shock that ended scarcity by ending the price controls and currency debasement causing it
Markets respond slowly to policy changes and the German recovery took a decade to begin, with the 1948 currency reform having no measurable effect during the first years after its enactment
Markets respond only to fiscal stimulus and the 1948 currency reform had no economic effect, with German recovery being driven by Marshall Plan aid disbursed over the subsequent years
The 1948 currency reform was never implemented and the Reichsmark remained Germany's currency until the introduction of the euro in 2002, with no Deutsche mark issuance taking place in 1948
context: Wilhelm Roepke (Hayek-aligned Austrian) was Erhard's intellectual influence. The Allied authorities tried to fire Erhard for unauthorized action; he could not be fired because he was technically not under their authority. The episode is a clean test of Hayekian arguments about markets, prices, and information.

question: In February 2022, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the US Treasury froze ~$300B in Russian central-bank reserves held at the Fed and ECB. The action was unprecedented: reserves had traditionally been treated as sovereign-immune. The dollar's reserve-currency status depends on this immunity. What did the freeze signal to other central banks?
answer: Holding reserves in any currency exposes the issuer to political risk if relations sour; the action sped up central-bank gold buying and dollar-alternative discussion among BRICS nations
choices: Holding reserves in any currency exposes the issuer to political risk if relations sour; the action sped up central-bank gold buying and dollar-alternative discussion among BRICS nations

The freeze had no signaling effect on other central banks and global reserve allocation has remained unchanged since 2022, with no measurable increase in central-bank gold purchases or dollar diversification

The freeze actually increased dollar demand because other central banks viewed it as evidence of US monetary strength, and dollar reserve share rose to record highs in the years following the 2022 sanctions
The Treasury reversed the freeze in months and Russian reserves were returned in full, with no consequences for the dollar's reserve-currency status or for central-bank confidence in US commitments
context: Central-bank gold purchases reached record levels in 2022-23. China, India, Turkey, and various Gulf states accelerated diversification. The deeper question (whether the dollar's reserve role is being slowly eroded) remains open. The freeze was a calculated weapon; the long-run cost may exceed the short-run gain.

question: The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 raised US tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods to the highest levels in over a century. Over 1,000 economists signed a petition urging Hoover to veto. He signed it. Global trade fell about 65% between 1929 and 1934. What does Smoot-Hawley illustrate about protectionism?
answer: Tariffs invite retaliation from trading partners, collapsing the cross-border specialization that gains-from-trade depends on, deepening rather than relieving the downturn that motivated the protection
choices: Tariffs invite retaliation from trading partners, collapsing the cross-border specialization that gains-from-trade depends on, deepening rather than relieving the downturn that motivated the protection

Tariffs always increase domestic employment and output, and Smoot-Hawley successfully protected US industry through the 1930s with no measurable negative effects on the US economy or its trading partners
Smoot-Hawley had no measurable effect on global trade and the 1929-1934 trade decline was caused entirely by unrelated demographic and currency factors with no link to US tariff policy
Smoot-Hawley was repealed in 1931 before having any effect and the 1930s decline in trade volume happened without any tariff barriers being in effect at any point in any major economy
context: Senator Reed Smoot (R-Utah) and Representative Willis Hawley (R-Oregon) championed the bill at the protectionist edge of the GOP. The 1000-economist petition was organized by Paul Douglas. Hoover signed despite the warning. Trade collapsed; the protected industries did not survive. Lessons widely ignored in subsequent tariff debates.

question: Beginning 2018, the Trump administration imposed tariffs on Chinese imports under Section 301, covering ~$370B in goods at 7.5-25% rates. China retaliated, particularly hitting US agricultural exports. The 2020 Phase One deal partially de-escalated. Studies (Amiti et al., Fajgelbaum et al.) found the tariffs were passed through to US consumers and producers. Who actually paid the tariffs?
answer: US consumers and producers paid via higher prices — the 'China is paying' framing was contradicted by every serious pass-through analysis
choices: US consumers and producers paid via higher prices — the 'China is paying' framing was contradicted by every serious pass-through analysis
Foreign exporters paid as Trump claimed — the 2018-19 tariffs successfully transferred wealth from China to the US with no cost to consumers or businesses
Nobody paid measurably — the 2018-19 tariffs had no measurable economic effect, with US prices and trade flows unchanged from pre-tariff baselines
Nobody paid anything — the 2018-19 tariffs were not actually implemented, with the Section 301 action being a media story without policy effect
context: The Biden administration largely maintained the Trump tariffs through 2024. Both parties moved toward protectionism. The Phase One deal's purchase commitments were not met. The political appeal of 'tough on China' framings outran the economic analysis of who actually pays the tax.

question: In 1845 Frederic Bastiat published 'The Petition of the Candle Makers', a satirical petition to the French Chamber of Deputies demanding protection from 'unfair competition' from a foreign rival, the sun. The candle makers argued blocking sunlight would create jobs for candle makers, shutter makers, oil producers. Bastiat's reductio was meant to expose what?
answer: Every protectionist argument can be applied to any competitor, including the sun; if 'creating jobs' justifies tariffs, it justifies any restriction however absurd, exposing the underlying fallacy
choices: Every protectionist argument can be applied to any competitor, including the sun; if 'creating jobs' justifies tariffs, it justifies any restriction however absurd, exposing the underlying fallacy
The petition was a sincere proposal from the French candle industry and was actually adopted by the Chamber of Deputies, with sunlight being restricted in France for several decades afterward

The petition argued for free trade with the sun and against protection of the candle industry, with Bastiat actually supporting tariffs against foreign manufactured goods despite his satirical framing

The petition was a serious economic analysis showing that sunlight competition really did hurt the French candle industry and that protection was a legitimate policy response to international solar trade
context: Bastiat's 'The Candlemakers' Petition' is anthologized in 'Economic Sophisms' (1845). The satire is one of the clearest expositions of the seen-and-unseen fallacy applied to trade. The candlemakers' argument structure recurs in every modern industry-protection lobby — exposed by Bastiat 180 years ago.

question: New York City has had rent control or rent stabilization since 1943, originally as a wartime measure. The Rent Control Law of 1947 made it permanent. By 2024 ~half of NYC apartments are rent-stabilized. Studies (Glaeser, Diamond) find the policy reduces tenant mobility, lowers maintenance, distorts allocation, and reduces new construction. Which Swedish socialist economist said rent control is the most efficient way to destroy a city — except for bombing?
answer: Assar Lindbeck — the seen benefit (current tenants pay less) concentrates; unseen costs (future renters, supply, maintenance) spread
choices: Assar Lindbeck — the seen benefit (current tenants pay less) concentrates; unseen costs (future renters, supply, maintenance) spread
Paul Krugman — rent control benefits all New Yorkers equally, and every NY economist across schools supports it as good policy
Joseph Stiglitz — NYC repealed rent control in 1970 and has operated under purely free-market housing ever since across all boroughs
Thomas Piketty — rent control INCREASES housing supply, and NYC has the highest per-capita construction rate among major US cities
context: Assar Lindbeck (Swedish socialist economist) once said 'in many cases rent control appears to be the most efficient technique presently known to destroy a city, except for bombing.' The literature is one of the strongest cross-school consensuses in applied economics.

question: Sweden has the strictest rent regulation of any developed economy. New tenants in Stockholm wait up to 20 years for a regulated apartment. The black market for sublet rent-controlled units is large. Most new tenancies happen through informal swaps, family transfers, or under-the-table payments. Why does Sweden's textbook case persist politically?
